When you panic, your head can go light.

clears a light head
Fainting happens when blood pressure drops. Right now yours has gone up, not down.
The light-headed feeling is fast breathing, not a warning. It eases as the out-breath gets longer.

Slower breathing is what settles your hands.

Breathing fast changes the mix of gases in your blood, and that makes hands, feet and lips tingle.

docs.title: Affirmation explanations
docs.body:
# The line, explained

What opens when somebody taps a check-in alert and then wants more. All
forty-four are written. Voice rules are `_docs/kind-writing-style.md`; the
lines themselves are `_docs/briefs/affirmation-lines.md`.

## What it is

A sheet that slides up over Home. The sidekick stays visible behind it, the
line is at the top, three short parts under it, and one way out.

Nothing is asked, nothing is answered, nothing is stored. Closing it puts the
reader back on Home with the same line still there.

**Reading it is optional and always was.** The line on the lock screen is the
whole message on its own. Somebody who never taps has missed nothing. This is
for the evening where somebody reads a line, thinks "is that actually true?",
and wants the answer.

## The shape comes from the source, not from me

Two drafts invented prose to explain each line and neither made sense. The
assertiveness handout already holds the explanation, sitting in the column
this file had been told to ignore.

`_docs/briefs/ASSERTIVENESS SKILLS TRAINING l.md` is two columns wide:

| Mistaken Traditional Assumption | Your LEGITIMATE Right |
| --- | --- |
| You should always try to accommodate others. If you don't, they won't be there when you need them. | You have the right to say "no." |

The right on its own is an assertion. **The pair is an argument**, and the
left-hand column is the useful half: it names the rule the reader is actually
running on. You cannot put down a belief you cannot see, which is why naming
it is the standard move in assertiveness training in the first place.

So every sheet is three short parts:

| Part | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| **The rule you were given** | The belief, in plainer words. Said as something handed to the reader, never as something they believe. Eight sheets say **What it sounds like** instead -- see the thought shapes below. |
| **Why it does not hold** | One reason, with a real example where there is one. |
| **Closer to the truth** | The line, said plainly. |

### Where the other seventeen came from

Only nineteen of the lines are rights with a handout row. The rest needed
their rule naming from somewhere, and the Centre for Clinical Interventions in
Perth publishes free clinical workbooks built on exactly the same two-column
idea.

Its *Building Self-Compassion* module, on barriers to self-compassion, lists
the beliefs that keep self-criticism running -- that criticism motivates you,
toughens you up, pushes you to excel, keeps you humble; and that kindness to
yourself would make you lazy, self-indulgent and undisciplined. It then gives
the counter-arguments, and two of them are used repeatedly below:

- **It is not the criticism that helps, it is taking action** -- and action is
  available without the criticism.
- **You would never say it to a friend or a child.** If it worked, you would.

`Rest is allowed before it is earned` and `Starting badly is still starting`
are both straight out of that material.

### This reverses an earlier rule, on purpose and only here

`_docs/briefs/affirmation-lines.md` says the mistaken-assumption column must
never be used, because a line that repeats a mistaken belief plants it. **That
still binds every lock-screen line and it is not changing.**

It does not bind the sheet, and the difference is consent. Somebody tapped to
get here. They are reading on purpose, with the app open, and the belief is
named in order to be answered in the next paragraph. A belief named and
answered is recognition. A belief dropped onto a lock screen with nothing
after it is the thing that was banned.

**The naming has to be careful.** It is always "the rule you were given",
never "you think" or "you believe". Nobody is told what is in their head.

## The nineteen rights

One per row of the handout. The left column is the rule, the right column is
what is true instead, and the middle paragraph is the only part that had to be
written.

### 1. You are allowed to come first sometimes.

> **The rule you were given**
> Putting your needs before other people's is selfish.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Selfish means always. Sometimes is not always. And if you never come first, you run out of things to give.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Your needs count too. Some of the time they can come first.

### 2. Getting things wrong is part of being a person.

> **The rule you were given**
> Making mistakes is shameful. You should have the right answer ready every time.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Nobody has the right answer every time. The ones who look like they do have had more practice.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You are allowed to get it wrong. Getting it wrong is how you find out how to do it.

### 3. You know how you feel better than anyone does.

> **The rule you were given**
> If people do not agree your feelings make sense, then your feelings must be wrong.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> A feeling is not a claim that needs proof. Other people did not live your life. They are missing most of it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You are the one who knows. Nobody else gets to decide.

### 4. Your opinion is yours to hold.

> **The rule you were given**
> Respect other people's views, especially if they are in charge. Keep your differences to yourself.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Respecting a view is not the same as taking it on. Being in charge does not make somebody right.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can hold your own view. You do not have to hand it over.

### 5. Changing your mind is allowed, even late.

> **The rule you were given**
> You should always be logical and consistent.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Being the same is not a virtue when the facts have changed. Sticking to a bad call to look steady costs more.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can change your mind. Knowing more is a good reason.

### 6. If something felt unfair, you are allowed to say so.

> **The rule you were given**
> Be flexible and adjust. Other people have their reasons, and it is rude to question them.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Sometimes they do have good reasons. Sometimes they do not. There is no way to tell without asking.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can say something felt unfair. Asking is not rude.

### 7. You can stop someone and ask what they meant.

> **The rule you were given**
> Never interrupt. Asking questions shows you did not understand.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Not asking does not hide it. The muddle stays, and it shows up later. Most people would rather be asked.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can stop someone and ask. It gives nothing away.

### 8. You can ask for things to be different.

> **The rule you were given**
> Do not rock the boat. It could get worse.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Not asking has an ending too, and it is that nothing changes. That one rarely gets counted. Asking is not pushing.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You are allowed to ask for a change.

### 9. You are allowed to need somebody.

> **The rule you were given**
> Do not take up people's time with your problems.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> People who care about you would rather know. Being there for each other is most of the point of having people.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can ask for help. Helping each other is what people are for.

### 10. Saying that something hurt is allowed.

> **The rule you were given**
> People do not want to hear that you feel bad, so keep it in.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Kept in, it does not go away. It goes quiet. And the person who hurt you cannot mend what they do not know about.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can say that it hurt.

### 11. You can listen to advice and still not take it.

> **The rule you were given**
> If somebody takes the time to advise you, take it seriously. They are usually right.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> They are guessing from outside your life. Advice often comes from somebody's own worries, or their own story. Yours may be nothing like it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can listen, say thank you, and not do it.

### 12. Wanting your work noticed is a fair thing to want.

> **The rule you were given**
> Knowing you did well should be enough. Nobody likes a show-off.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Doing well and being noticed are two different things. Wanting the second one does not make you a show-off.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can want your work seen. You can even say so.

### 13. You can say no, and leave it at that.

> **The rule you were given**
> Always fit in with people. If you do not, they will not be there later.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Saying no once does not end a friendship. And when you give a reason, the reason is what people argue with. "You could come for just an hour."
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can say no. You do not have to say why.

### 14. It is alright to want the evening to yourself.

> **The rule you were given**
> Do not be antisocial. Say you would rather be alone and people will think you do not like them.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Wanting time alone is about you, not about them. Most people want it too.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can want an evening on your own.

### 15. "I would rather not" is reason enough.

> **The rule you were given**
> You should always have a good reason for what you feel and do.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Some things you just do not want to do. There is no better reason underneath. Looking for one takes longer than saying it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You do not have to explain yourself. "I'd rather not" is a real answer.

### 16. Not every problem near you is yours to solve.

> **The rule you were given**
> When somebody is in trouble, you should help them.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> You can care about somebody without taking their problem on. Taking it on can stop them solving it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can be there without carrying it.

### 17. You are not expected to guess what people need.

> **The rule you were given**
> Be sensitive to what people want, even when they do not tell you.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Nobody can read minds. Guessing goes wrong, and guessing all day is tiring. People can say what they want.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You do not have to work it out in advance.

### 18. Not everybody has to be pleased with you today.

> **The rule you were given**
> It is always a good policy to stay on people's good side.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> You cannot. It would mean agreeing with everyone, and they do not agree with each other. People do not have to agree to like each other.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Some days people are annoyed and you never find out why. Often it has nothing to do with you.

### 19. Not every message needs an answer tonight.

> **The rule you were given**
> It is not nice to leave people waiting. If you are asked, answer.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Most messages are not urgent. And a tired reply is the worse reply.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can reply tomorrow.

## The other seventeen

No handout row, so the rule had to be named first. Most of them are already
described in the CCI self-compassion module as beliefs that keep self-criticism
running: that criticism motivates, that rest is a reward, that kindness makes
you lazy.

### 20. Hard is allowed to be hard.

> **The rule you were given**
> If you were coping properly, this would not feel hard.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Hard things are hard for everybody. Struggling with one tells you about the thing, not about you.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> It can be hard and you can be fine.

### 21. Tired does not need a reason.

> **The rule you were given**
> You are only allowed to be tired if you can show what tired you out.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Some days you are just tired. There is no reason you can point to. It is still real.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You do not have to prove it.

### 22. Invisible work is still work.

> **The rule you were given**
> Work counts when somebody can see it.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Most of what wears people out leaves no trace. Worrying, planning, keeping the peace, holding it together at work.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> It counted. Nobody had to see it.

### 23. You are allowed to feel exactly this much.

> **The rule you were given**
> Your feelings should match the size of the thing.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Feelings do not arrive measured. And "you're overreacting" is what people say when they want the feeling to stop.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You feel what you feel. There is no correct amount.

### 24. Today is allowed to be a slow one.

> **The rule you were given**
> A day should produce something.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> That is a rule about work, used on a life. Nobody makes something every day. The ones who look like they do are not showing you all of it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Some days are slow. That is a day, not a failure.

### 25. You can take up as much room as you need.

> **The rule you were given**
> Do not be a burden. Take up less space.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> People who like you are not keeping count. That is not how liking somebody works.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You are allowed to take up room.

### 26. Rest is allowed before it is earned.

> **The rule you were given**
> Rest is what you get after you finish.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Bodies do not work like that. Resting when you are tired is how more gets done, not less.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can rest now. You do not have to have earned it.

### 27. Tonight does not have to sort out tomorrow.

> **The rule you were given**
> If you do not work it out now, you will be caught out.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Going over a problem at night rarely solves it. It just runs it again. The morning is a better time to think.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> It can wait until tomorrow.

### 28. It is a human way to feel.

> **The rule you were given**
> Other people do not feel like this. Something is wrong with you.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Other people's insides are not on show. Only yours are, to you. That is not a fair match, and everybody makes it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Plenty of people feel exactly this. Right now.

### 29. A thought showed up. You did not choose it.

> **The rule you were given**
> A thought is yours, so it says something about you.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Minds throw up all sorts. Some of it you disagree with. Having a thought is not the same as picking it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> A thought arriving tells you nothing about who you are.

### 30. Minds wander. That is what minds do.

> **The rule you were given**
> A mind that wanders is a mind you have lost control of.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Minds do this all day. Everybody's does. So does the mind of somebody who has meditated for years.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> A wandering mind is a mind working the way minds work.

### 31. You do not have to answer every thought.

> **The rule you were given**
> A thought that turns up is addressed to you and wants an answer.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> You cannot stop thoughts showing up. That part is not up to you. But you do not have to deal with each one.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can notice a thought and carry on with what you were doing.

### 32. You got through today. Nothing more was needed.

> **The rule you were given**
> Getting through a day does not count as doing anything.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Some days, getting through it is the work. It takes something. Nobody sees it. It still happened.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You got to the end of it. That was enough.

### 33. Starting badly is still starting.

> **The rule you were given**
> If you cannot do it properly, do not start.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Nothing starts well. The good version is a bad version that got worked on.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> A bad start is still a start. Starting when you know it will be rough is the harder version.

### 34. Half done still counts.

> **The rule you were given**
> Unfinished means it does not count.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Half the washing up is half less washing up. It does not come back because you stopped.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> What you did is still done.

### 35. Slow is still forward.

> **The rule you were given**
> If it is not fast, it is not progress.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Speed is a comparison. Progress is not. Something moving slowly is still moving.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Slow still counts as forward.

### 36. The chair is holding you. Let it do the work.

> **The rule you were given**
> You have to hold yourself up.
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> The chair is already doing it. Most people hold their shoulders and back tight all day and never notice. They are holding up something already held.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can stop holding. It has you.

## The eight thought shapes

Drawn from `_docs/briefs/17 UNHELPFUL THINKING STYLES.md`, which is Leahy's
list of cognitive distortions. A different shape of source, so a different
shape of sheet.

The assertiveness handout names a **rule about how to behave**. This one names
a **shape a thought takes**. There is no rule to put in the first part, so
these sheets open with the thought itself, under "What it sounds like".

### These must never diagnose

The biggest risk in the whole file lives here, and it is worth stating
plainly. **Naming a distortion is telling the reader their thinking is
faulty.** "You are catastrophising" is a diagnosis, delivered by an app, to
somebody having a hard evening, about the inside of their own head. It breaks
the oldest rule in these files: never tell the reader something about
themselves that the app cannot know.

Three rules follow, and all eight sheets hold them:

- **The shape is never named.** Not "catastrophising", not "mind reading", not
  "overgeneralising". The words do not appear anywhere the reader can see.
- **The sheet describes the thought, never the thinker.** "A guess about
  tomorrow is still a guess" is about the guess. "You always assume the
  worst" would be about the reader, and it would be wrong as often as right.
- **The thought is quoted, not attributed.** The first part is in quotation
  marks, as a sentence somebody might hear, never as "what you are telling
  yourself".

### One was written and thrown away

**Emotional reasoning** -- treating a feeling as proof of a fact -- is on the
source list and is not here.

It contradicts line 6, "You know how you feel better than anyone does",
which tells the reader they are the authority on their own feelings. The real
distinction is between the feeling being genuine and the feeling proving
something about the world, and that difference is too fine to carry on a lock
screen. Got wrong, it reads as the app telling somebody their feelings are
not to be trusted, which is the opposite of what line 6 exists to say.

### 37. Once is not always.

> **What it sounds like**
> "That always happens to me." "I always get this wrong."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> One time is one time. "Always" turns up to protect you. It is trying to get you ready for next time, so it makes one go sound like a rule.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> It happened once. That is all you know so far.

### 38. Most things are not all or nothing.

> **What it sounds like**
> "It was a complete waste of time." "Nobody likes me."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Almost nothing is all of anything. Most of it sits in the middle, and the middle is harder to see when you are tired.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Most things are a mix. Some of it went badly. Some of it did not.

### 39. A guess about tomorrow is still a guess.

> **What it sounds like**
> "It is going to go badly. I already know how this ends."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Nobody can see tomorrow. A guess made on a bad evening sounds far more certain than it is.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You do not know yet, and nor does anybody else. Tomorrow can be dealt with tomorrow.

### 40. A what-if has no answer that will do.

> **What it sounds like**
> "But what if it goes wrong? What if I cannot cope?"
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Answer one and another one turns up. No answer settles it. What the question wants is to be certain, and certain is not something anybody gets.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You can leave the question sitting there.

### 41. You cannot know what they were thinking.

> **What it sounds like**
> "They think I am an idiot. They were annoyed with me."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> Nobody can see inside somebody else's head. A guess made on a bad day tends to be the unkind one.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You do not know. Nobody can know what somebody else is thinking.

### 42. You cannot go back and do it differently.

> **What it sounds like**
> "I should have said something else. I should have known."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> That judges an old decision using what you know now. You did not know it then. It is not a fair test.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You did it with what you had at the time.

### 43. One bad go is not a description of you.

> **What it sounds like**
> "I am useless. I am a bad friend."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> A whole person does not fit in one word. And that word only shows up after something goes wrong. It never shows up after something goes well.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> Something went badly. That is the size of it. (That is the size of it doesn't feel like it says anything)

### 44. It still counts, even if it was easy.

> **What it sounds like**
> "That does not count. Anybody could have done that."
>
> **Why it does not hold**
> "Anybody could have done it" is a way of making it smaller. It still needed doing, and you are the one who did it.
>
> **Closer to the truth**
> You did it. That is the whole test.

## Two notes from the review

**"Learning from mistakes helps us grow" was asked for and written carefully.**
Sheet 2 now ends "Getting it wrong is how you find out how to do it." The
obvious version -- *mistakes are how we grow* -- puts a condition back on:
if a mistake is alright because you learned from it, then a mistake you
learned nothing from is still shameful, which is the rule the sheet is
answering. The wording above makes getting it wrong part of the method, not
the price of being forgiven.

**Nine sheets stopped assuming things about the reader.** One was caught in
review and the other eight came out of an audit of all thirty-six afterwards.
It is the file's oldest rule, arriving in a new disguise: never tell the
reader something about themselves that the app cannot know.

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| Somebody is annoyed with you. | Some days people are annoyed and you never find out why. |
| You just stay lost. | The confusion stays. |
| …which is the thing you are unhappy about. | …which is the other outcome nobody counts. |
| And you would want them to tell you. | Most people would want to be told, if it were the other way round. |
| When you try you get it wrong, and it wears you out. | Guessing goes wrong, and guessing all day is tiring. |
| An answer given when you are empty. | A tired reply. |
| The counting is happening in your head. | That is not how liking somebody works. |
| Tomorrow you will know more and be awake. | The morning is a better time to think. |
| You see other people's outsides and your own insides. | Other people's insides are not on show. Only yours are, to you. |

The pattern in every one of them is the same. The sentence was true of most
people most of the time, which is exactly what makes it easy to write and easy
to miss. It still lands as the app telling somebody what is going on in their
head, their week or their body, and the app does not know.

**The sheet that started it.** A draft
said "somebody is annoyed with you", which quietly hands the reader
responsibility for a mood they had no part in. People are annoyed for their
own reasons and usually never say which, so the sheet now says that instead.
It is the same rule as the one behind the whole file: never tell the reader
something about themselves that the app cannot know.

**Two lines changed, not just their sheets.** "A thought turned up. You did
not order it" became "A thought showed up. You did not choose it" -- ordering
is something you do in a shop, and choosing is the actual point. "Half of it
done is a real amount" became "Half done still counts", which is what
somebody would say out loud.

## Seven lines were cut writing this

Each one failed the same test: no rule behind it, or a rule already answered
by a line that does it better. A line with no rule behind it cannot have a
sheet, and a set where some lines open something and others do not is a set
where tapping is a gamble.

| Cut | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Some days ask for more than they say they will. | The nearest rule is "you should be able to predict what a day will cost", which nobody actually believes. |
| Carrying something quietly is still carrying it. | Same rule as "Invisible work is still work", which says it better. |
| If today was a lot, that makes sense. | A conditional kindness, not a belief. Nothing to argue with. |
| It is fine to want an easy evening. | Same rule as "Today is allowed to be a slow one" and "It is alright to want the evening to yourself". |
| Nobody gets through a week without a bad hour. | Same rule as "It is a human way to feel". |
| You are the room, not the weather in it. | A metaphor, which rule 4 of the style guide bans. It was the only one left in the set. |
| Starting with the small things is a real plan. | Same rule as "Starting badly is still starting", which says it better. |

## Every sheet says what family it is from

Added 19 September 2026. A small label above the line, so the reader can see
what kind of thing they have opened before they read it.

| Category | Lines |
| --- | --- |
| When it was hard | 3 |
| Things you're allowed | 19 |
| Your own pace | 5 |
| Other people feel this too | 1 |
| When a thought won't go | 11 |
| Small still counts | 4 |
| Your body | 1 |

**No category names the technique behind it.** Not "assertiveness training",
not "cognitive distortions", not "self-compassion". A category is there to
orient somebody, not to tell them which textbook they are in -- and a reader
who learns they are doing CBT at 8:30 pm has been handed a fact about the app
rather than about themselves. A test pins that the words never appear.

The category also answers a worry recorded twice in
`_docs/briefs/affirmation-lines.md`: that a set where every line teaches reads
as a course. A visible label makes that more obvious, not less, and it is a
fair trade -- somebody who can see the seven families can tell that the app is
not repeating itself, which is the thing a course actually feels like.

## The third heading is "Closer to the truth"

It was "What is true instead". That claims the last word, and most of these
sheets are about nuance rather than swapping one certainty for another -- the
all-or-nothing sheet in particular says most things are a mix, under a heading
announcing what is true. The heading undid the sheet that earned it.

## Built

The sheet is `lib/features/dashboard/widgets/affirmation_sheet.dart` and the
words are in `lib/features/dashboard/models/affirmation_explanations.dart`,
generated from this file.

Two of the open questions below were answered while building:

- **The three headings are on screen.** They carry the argument, and without
  them the three parts run together into one paragraph that reads as a
  lecture.
- **The line on Home is tappable.** Nothing marks it as a button -- somebody
  who only wants to read the line should not be handed a thing to press -- but
  it means the writing is reachable without waiting for an evening alert.
  Easily reversed if Home starts feeling like something to read rather than
  something to look at.

A test pins that every line in the set has an explanation and that no
explanation exists for a line that is not in the set. That is what stops the
two files drifting apart, which nothing else would catch.

## Open questions

- **Does the sheet want the character in it, or only behind it?** She is on
  Home underneath. Putting her inside as well would be two of her.
- **The rights are still nineteen of thirty-six.** Over half. It was already
  the largest group and the cuts fell elsewhere again.

## Sources

- `_docs/briefs/ASSERTIVENESS SKILLS TRAINING l.md`, the legitimate-rights
  table. The tradition runs back to Smith's assertive-rights work in the
  1970s and it is still the standard handout.
- Centre for Clinical Interventions, *Building Self-Compassion*, Module 2:
  Barriers to Self-Compassion.
  https://www.cci.health.wa.gov.au/Resources/Looking-After-Yourself/Self-Compassion
- Centre for Clinical Interventions, *Improving Self-Esteem*, on rules and
  assumptions.
  https://www.cci.health.wa.gov.au/resources/looking-after-yourself/self-esteem

docs.title: Affirmation lines
docs.body:
# Affirmation lines

The lines Home pairs with a pose, and the lines the daily check-in carries in
its own notification text. One set, two readers: somebody who opened the app,
and somebody glancing at a lock screen at 8:30 pm.

Rewritten 19 September 2026, from psychology rather than from philosophy.

## Why this was rewritten

The first two drafts were built from Stoic and then Buddhist material, and
both failed the same way. They were assembled by **subtraction** -- every rule
in the file removed something, so nearly every line removed something too.
"Nothing has to be fixed." "You do not have to believe it." "There is nothing
to finish." Each line is defensible and the set is cold. A reader at 8:30 pm
is handed a list of things that are not required of them, which is not the
same as being handed anything.

A kind affirmation **gives**. Warmth, permission, company, or the plain
acknowledgement that today was hard. That is what this draft is built to do.

## What the psychology actually says

Four findings do all the work here.

### Praise-shaped affirmations hurt the people who need them

Wood, Perunovic and Lee (*Psychological Science*, 2009) had people repeat "I
am a lovable person". People with **low self-esteem felt worse afterwards**,
and worse than a control group who repeated nothing. The statement is so far
from what they believe that saying it starts an argument they lose.

This is the single most important finding for this feature, and it is what
rules out a whole genre:

| Ruled out | Why |
| --- | --- |
| You are enough. | A verdict, and it can be disagreed with. |
| You are doing better than you think. | A claim about the reader that may be plainly false tonight. |
| You are strong. / You've got this. | Praise. Starts the argument Wood found. |
| Believe in yourself. | Homework, and a trait claim. |

Everything above was in the reader's own placeholder set or in common
affirmation apps. None of it survives.

### Kindness works where praise fails

Neff's self-compassion work, and the MacBeth and Gumley meta-analysis
(*Clinical Psychology Review*, 2012), point the other way: **treating
yourself as you would treat somebody you like** tracks better mental health,
where self-esteem boosting does not. Kindness makes no claim about the
reader's worth, so there is nothing to disagree with.

So the lines are kind, not complimentary. "I hope today is easy" cannot be
refuted. "You are amazing" can.

### Validation beats reassurance

Linehan's validation work, and the whole of motivational interviewing, find
that naming somebody's experience accurately lands where reassurance bounces.
"That was a lot to carry" is heard. "It will be fine" is not.

The old draft had almost no validation in it. This one leads with it.

### Affirm a value, not a trait

Self-affirmation theory (Steele, 1988; Cohen and Sherman, *Annual Review*,
2014) has hundreds of studies behind it, and the effect comes from affirming
something the person **cares about** -- not from affirming that they are good
at something. "The things that matter to you still matter" is a value. "You
are capable" is a trait, and a trait can be argued with.

### The app does not know what kind of day it was

Added 19 September 2026, after the third draft. The validation group asserted
a hard day outright -- "That took something out of you. Of course it did." --
and the alert fires **every** evening, on fine days too.

Three things go wrong at once:

| Problem | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| It is often simply untrue | Most days are ordinary. A line insisting today was heavy is wrong more often than right. |
| Inaccurate validation stops working | Validation lands because it is accurate. Linehan's point is that a wrong reading is heard as not being listened to, which is the thing validation exists to fix. |
| It frames a fine day as a bad one | Read over a fortnight, it is an app that thinks the reader is fragile -- and it offers a bad-day reading to somebody who did not have one. |

So no line may assert what today was like. Lines either describe nothing about
the day, say something general and true on any day, or offer a reading
**conditionally** -- "If today was a lot, that makes sense."

**A group of ordinary-day lines was written for this and then cut in the
fourth draft.** See the open questions: the rule above is still held by every
line, but nothing in the set now speaks to a day that went fine.

## The two rules that stayed

Most of the previous draft's bans were my own over-caution and are lifted.
Two are not, and both are safety rules rather than style ones.

1. **No breath instructions.** Not "take a deep breath", not "notice your
   breath". Stretching the in-breath is what hyperventilation looks like, and
   a panic reader may open the app straight after reading one of these lines.
   This is the one ban in the app with a randomised trial behind it.
2. **No promises about tomorrow.** "This will pass", "it gets better". The app
   cannot keep them, and a promise broken by the next bad night costs more
   than the line ever gave.

Everything else -- metaphor, warmth, the word "you", a line that gives an
instruction gently -- is allowed. Lines may run to about twelve words where
warmth needs the room.

## The lines

Forty-four. Grouped by what each one gives.

### It may have been hard -- validation that does not presume

1. Hard is allowed to be hard.
2. Tired does not need a reason.
3. Invisible work is still work.

### Things you are allowed, with other people -- the rights

4. You are allowed to come first sometimes.
5. Getting things wrong is part of being a person.
6. You know how you feel better than anyone does.
7. Your opinion is yours to hold.
8. Changing your mind is allowed, even late.
9. If something felt unfair, you are allowed to say so.
10. You can stop someone and ask what they meant.
11. You can ask for things to be different.
12. You are allowed to need somebody.
13. Saying that something hurt is allowed.
14. You can listen to advice and still not take it.
15. Wanting your work noticed is a fair thing to want.
16. You can say no, and leave it at that.
17. It is alright to want the evening to yourself.
18. "I would rather not" is reason enough.
19. Not every problem near you is yours to solve.
20. You are not expected to guess what people need.
21. Not everybody has to be pleased with you today.
22. Not every message needs an answer tonight.

### Your own pace -- permission

23. You are allowed to feel exactly this much.
24. Today is allowed to be a slow one.
25. You can take up as much room as you need.
26. Rest is allowed before it is earned.
27. Tonight does not have to sort out tomorrow.

### Somebody else, right now -- common humanity

28. It is a human way to feel.

### Thoughts arrive on their own -- holding them loosely

29. A thought showed up. You did not choose it.
30. Minds wander. That is what minds do.
31. You do not have to answer every thought.
32. Once is not always.
33. Most things are not all or nothing.
34. A guess about tomorrow is still a guess.
35. A what-if has no answer that will do.
36. You cannot know what they were thinking.
37. You cannot go back and do it differently.
38. One bad go is not a description of you.
39. It still counts, even if it was easy.

### Small is real -- behavioural activation

40. You got through today. Nothing more was needed.
41. Starting badly is still starting.
42. Half done still counts.
43. Slow is still forward.

### Weight and warmth -- the body, kindly

44. The chair is holding you. Let it do the work.

## What each group gives

| Group | Gives | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1-3 | Being believed, without being told what today was | Validation: Linehan, motivational interviewing |
| 4-22 | A standing permission about other people | Assertiveness training's legitimate rights |
| 23-27 | Permission about your own pace | Removes an internal conflict rather than a task |
| 28 | Not being alone in it | Neff's common humanity |
| 29-39 | Room to leave a thought alone | Defusion, and the seventeen unhelpful thinking styles |
| 40-43 | A size that is doable | Behavioural activation's smallest-step finding |
| 44 | Physical rest | Weight and contact, the Low script's anchors |

**Every line now has an explanation behind it**, written in
`_docs/briefs/affirmation-explanations.md`. That is why the last seven cuts
happened: a line with no rule behind it cannot carry one, and a set where
some lines open something and others do not makes tapping a gamble.

**Validation comes first on purpose.** Somebody who feels believed can hear
the rest. Somebody handed a correction before being believed hears it as
being argued with.

## The warmth group was written, then cut

Two drafts were spent on this and both are worth recording, because the
argument will come round again.

**The ordinary-day lines went first.** "An ordinary day is a perfectly good
day", "Nothing much happened. That is allowed to be nice." They had the same
fault as the hard-day lines they were written to balance, pointing the other
way: they classified today, and the app cannot know what today was.

**The wishes replaced them and then went too.** "I hope tonight is a soft
one", "I am glad you are here", "Hello. I was thinking about you." A wish
claims nothing, so it was safe on any day, and that was the right fix for the
problem in front of it.

It was cut on 19 September 2026 for a different reason. **Tapping an alert
now opens an explanation** -- see `_docs/briefs/affirmation-explanations.md`
-- and a warmth line has nothing to explain. Writing one anyway produces
filler, and filler is what makes an app feel fake. So every line in the set
now has a lesson behind it, and the tap always does the same thing.

**What this costs, stated plainly.** Nothing in the set speaks to a day that
simply went fine, and every line now teaches something. A set that is all
instruction is the failure mode the second draft had, and the warmth group
was the counterweight. If the set ever starts reading as a course rather than
a friend, this decision is the first place to look.

## Why the rights group is the strongest in the file

Lines 4 to 22 come from the legitimate-rights table in
`_docs/briefs/ASSERTIVENESS SKILLS TRAINING l.md`, one line per right. That
tradition runs back to Smith's assertive-rights work in the 1970s, and it is
still the standard handout in assertiveness training.

It clears all three traps this file has hit, which nothing else in the set
manages at once:

| Trap | Why a right clears it |
| --- | --- |
| Praise backfires (Wood 2009) | A right makes no claim about the reader's worth. There is nothing to disagree with, because it is not about how good they are. |
| The app cannot know what kind of day it was | A right is true on a fine Tuesday and a terrible one. It never asserts anything about today. |
| Subtraction reads cold | A right **grants** rather than removes. "You can say no, and leave it at that" hands the reader something. |

There is a fourth reason, and it may be the most useful. **Most evening
distress is about other people** -- something that was said, something agreed
to and now regretted, a message not yet answered. Every other group in this
file speaks to the reader alone. This group is the only one that speaks to the
room they were actually in.

### Written warm, not legal

The source says "You have the right to...". That construction is kept out of
every line.

| Source | Here | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You have the right to say "no." | You can say no, and leave it at that. | "Right" implies somebody grants it, and somebody could refuse. A plain statement needs no permission-giver. |
| You have a right not to have to justify yourself to others. | "I would rather not" is reason enough. | The source names an absence. The line hands over a sentence the reader can actually use. |
| You have a right not to take responsibility for someone else's problem. | Not every problem near you is yours to solve. | Blunt, this reads as permission to abandon people. "Near you" keeps the person in the room. |
| It is selfish to put your needs before others' needs. | You are allowed to come first sometimes. | The source states the mistaken belief in order to argue with it. A line that repeats a mistaken belief plants it. Only the right is used, never the assumption beside it. |

**Ten of the nineteen avoid the word "allowed" entirely**, because nineteen
permissions in a row all built the same way becomes a tic rather than a voice.

## Still left out, and why

| Rejected | Why |
| --- | --- |
| You are enough. / You are stronger than you know. | Wood 2009. Praise-shaped, and it backfires on low self-esteem. |
| You are doing better than you think. | Same. A claim the reader can flatly disagree with. |
| This will pass. / Tomorrow is a new day. | A promise the app cannot keep. |
| Take a deep breath. / Notice your breath. | The one ban with a trial behind it. |
| It is not your fault. / You are not broken. | The reader has to build the fault to hear the line. |
| Everything happens for a reason. | Assigns meaning to somebody's bad night on their behalf. |
| Choose happiness. / Good vibes only. | Makes the feeling a failure of will. |
| You showed up today. | A mark out of ten dressed as kindness, and false on a lock screen nobody tapped. |
| That took something out of you. Of course it did. | Third draft. Asserts a hard day the app cannot know about. Survives conditionally as line 7. |
| It makes sense that you are tired. / Anybody would be worn out after that. | Same fault. "After what?" on an ordinary Tuesday. |
| You have been managing something invisible all day. | Same fault, and it is the most specific of the three, so the most often wrong. Survives as line 4, stated generally. |
| Nothing is asked of you here. | A subtraction line that slipped through, and it plants the idea that things are asked. |
| *(whole group)* An ordinary day is a perfectly good day. / Nothing much happened. That is allowed to be nice. / If something good happened, it still happened. | Cut in the fourth draft. Raised again in the open questions -- nothing in the set now speaks to a day that went fine. |
| *(whole group)* The things that matter to you still matter. / What you love has not gone anywhere. | Cut in the fourth draft. This was the self-affirmation group, and it was the most abstract writing in the file, so the cut is defensible. The evidence behind it is not replaced by anything else here. |
| Right now, somebody else is feeling exactly this. / Plenty of people are having this exact evening. / You are in ordinary company tonight. | Cut in the fourth draft, leaving common humanity with two lines. |
| Come back whenever. The light stays on. | Cut in the fourth draft. |
| Seven more, listed in `_docs/briefs/affirmation-explanations.md` | Cut in the seventh draft. Each had no rule behind it, or a rule that a better line already answers, so none could carry an explanation sheet. |
| *(whole group)* I am glad you are here. / I hope you are alright. / Hello. I was thinking about you. / I hope tonight is a soft one. | Cut in the sixth draft, once tapping an alert opened an explanation. There is no lesson in a warmth line, and writing one anyway is filler. See the section above for what this costs. |

## The four existing placeholders

All four are cut. Two are praise-shaped, one scores the reader, and one
survives as line 43.

| Existing line | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| You are doing better than you think. | Cut -- praise-shaped. |
| Nothing has to be fixed right now. | Cut -- the subtraction shape this draft moved away from. Line 27 gives the same permission warmly. |
| You came back. That counts. | Cut -- scores the reader, and means nothing to somebody who has not come back. |
| Slow is still forward. | Kept, line 43. |

## Open questions

- **The rights are nineteen of forty-four.** No longer over half. The thoughts
  group growing from three lines to eleven is what fixed it, rather than
  trimming the rights, which is the better of the two ways.
- **Every line now teaches.** That is the point of the last two rounds of
  cuts, and it is also the risk: a set that only instructs reads as a course
  rather than a friend. Watch for it.
- **Common humanity is one line.** Thin for the idea the Low script leans on
  hardest, and now the smallest group by some way.
- **Lines 19 and 22** -- "Not every problem near you is yours to solve" and
  "Not every message needs an answer tonight" -- are permission to step back.
  For the wrong reader on the wrong night they could read as permission to
  withdraw from everybody, and the warmth that balanced them is gone.

docs.title: Answer poses brief
docs.body:
# Answers — the bob and the wince

What the sidekick does when a Practice lesson's score lands. Two poses,
shared by every lesson under Practice.

Written 21 September 2026. Rig checked against `assets/rive/character.riv` the
same day. The Dart side is built: `AnswerPose`
(`lib/features/practice/models/answer_pose.dart`) fires the triggers, and an
unbuilt trigger is a no-op, so the lessons already run correctly on her idle.

---

## Deleted, then brought back on a different axis — 22 September 2026

`AnswerPose` was deleted on 21 September 2026, hours after this brief was
written, and everything below was left in place as the record of why the poses
exist. It came back on 22 September 2026. **The poses did not change. When
they fire did**, and that is the whole difference:

| | The deleted version | The current one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fires | After every marked tap, up to 7 times a sitting | Once, on the score step |
| Reacting to | One answer | The run of seven, which the reader pressed "See how that went" to see |
| Reads as | The app marking you, repeatedly, in a lesson about criticism | The app saying how it went, once, because you asked |
| Tiresome by | The fourth — this brief said so | There is no fourth |

**Per-answer reactions stay deleted, and that is not reopened by this.** The
score step is the only pose in the whole drill.

**Updated 23 September 2026: the sorting steps have no face of their own
either.** They used to drive her off `LessonFace` — the *sentence's* own face,
a criticism making her cross and an "I" sentence leaving her flat — which was
defensible as reporting what the words do rather than marking the reader. It
went because the six sentences here sort cleanly and a real one rarely does:
the same words land differently by speaker, tone, relationship and week, so a
face pronouncing on one sorted sentence teaches that the sorting is a property
of sentences, and the reader takes that into a conversation where it is not
true. She now wears `LessonFace.neutral` for the whole of every graded
question, the fix included. The cards still carry the mark in green and red,
and the explanation panel — which can say "it depends", where a face cannot —
does the teaching.

**The score step is `SwapStepKind.score`**, between the fix and the sentence
builder. `SwapDrillScript.passMark` is 5 of 7: a perfect run was rejected
because at 7 of 7 the wince becomes the ordinary ending, which is the app
wincing at nearly everybody.

**The page around her is neutral — no tint, no tick, no tone.** Green and red
are verdicts on a sentence everywhere else in the drill; a whole page of either
is a verdict on the reader. The number is the page's own ink for the same
reason. Her shoulders carry the news, which is what these two poses are for.

**Everything below still governs the poses themselves**, the shoulders-up rule
above all.

---

## Where she is when this fires

> **Superseded on 21 September 2026.** Her window is **140 × 180** on the
> sorting steps and **190 × 150 of head only** on the finish. See "she is 180
> tall now" at the end. The section below is kept because it is what the two
> poses were designed against, and it is why the sparks exist.

The swap drill (`Routes.swapDrill`, "When something's bothering you") is
the first caller. She sits in an **88 × 104** box at the top left with a
speech bubble beside her, inside an `IgnorePointer` so a thumb reaching for
the answer cards underneath cannot set her jumping.

Two things follow from that size, and they decide the whole brief:

- **The head is the picture.** At 88 wide her head is roughly 48 pixels and
  her feet are about four. Anything below the shoulders is silhouette only.
- **It fires up to seven times in one sitting** — six sentences to sort, then
  one fix to pick. A reaction that is big the first time is tiresome by the
  fourth. Both poses are deliberately half the size they want to be.

---

## Neither pose is a verdict

The drill already has this rule written down, on `SwapCard.why`:

> It explains the sentence, never the reader: a wrong pick is told what the
> sentence does, not what they missed.

The cards carry the answer in green and red, and those two colours are fixed
literals precisely so nothing can soften or recolour them. The verdict is
therefore **already fully delivered** before she moves. Her job is the other
one: staying warm while it lands.

This matters most in this lesson, because this lesson is about criticism. A
character who visibly deflates when you pick wrong is the app doing the thing
the lesson is teaching you to spot.

| | She may | She may not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right | A small pleased bob, sparks beside her head | Applaud, cheer, jump |
| Wrong | A wince — shoulders **up**, eyes squeezed, head pulled back | Slump, frown, shake her head, look away |

**Shoulders up, never down.** Up is "ooh, that one stings" and it is shared
with the reader. Down is disappointment and it is aimed at them. The two poses
are two frames apart to build and a world apart to read.

---

## What the rig can actually do

Checked, not assumed. Both characters live stacked in the one `sidekick`
artboard, swapped by opacity. Mochi is the girl, Maui the cat.

| Part | Mochi | Maui | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Eyes | Yes | Yes | Four-point paths. The vertices can be keyed, so a happy `^` arc and a squeezed wince are both reachable with no new art |
| Brows | **Yes** | **No** | Mochi's have root bones. Maui has none, and adding some was tried and looked wrong -- see the wince below |
| Eye path vertices | Yes | Yes | Four cubic points, all animatable. This is what makes Maui's half-lid possible |
| Whiskers | No | **Yes** | Maui's own brows, effectively. Mirrored, so the left is authored around r 180 |
| `mouth-open` | Yes | Yes | One shape, already in the file, hidden at rest. Used by SayHi |
| Smile line | Drawn into her face | Separate `smile` node, two strokes | Different between them; key whichever each one has |
| `mouth-open` at rest | **Visible** (opacity 100) -- it *is* her mouth | Hidden (opacity 0) -- the alternate mouth | So the wince reshapes hers in place, and swaps his in |
| Shoulders | Yes | Yes | `RootBone` per arm, plus a forearm bone |
| Paws | Yes | Yes | Bone-driven only. **They barely read** — see below. The *arm* reads; the hand does not |
| Teeth | **No** | **No** | Nothing anywhere |
| Jaw | No | No | Mouth shapes only |

Three rules follow, and the first is the real cost of the work:

- **Every pose is authored twice**, once on each character's parts. The keys
  port across by part name, but the silhouettes differ and the amplitudes have
  to be re-checked on each.
- **The wince cannot lean on brows**, because half the cast has none. Brows are
  a bonus on Mochi, never the thing carrying the pose. Eyes and shoulders carry
  it on both.
- **Nothing is asked of the paws.** They are skinned to bones and ignore their
  own transforms, so a hand gesture comes out as a blob. The shoulder reads;
  the hand does not.

---

## The sparks

Three short strokes that fan out from behind her right ear on a right answer,
hold, and fade.

**Not above her head, and that is measured rather than chosen.** The artboard
is cropped tight to her ears -- they reach y 20 of 500 -- so there is no room
over her head for anything. The top-right corner is clear on both characters,
which is where they went. It is also where the reference images put them.

They are the most valuable thing in this brief and the cheapest. At 88 pixels
a facial expression is nearly illegible and a mark above the silhouette is
unmissable — which is the whole reason the reference images use them.

**They are drawn once, not twice.** Both characters stand in the same place
with their heads at the same height, so one set of strokes sits beside either
of them. They belong to the artboard, not to a character, and they are the
one part of this job that does not double.

Rules:

- Opacity 0 at rest, and in both skin timelines. They must never be visible
  on Home, on the breathing screen, or in the idle.
- **No *spark* on a wrong answer.** A spark for a wrong answer is a buzzer. The
  sweat drop is the opposite thing -- it is her reacting, not the app scoring.
- Three strokes, uneven lengths, uneven angles. Four is a firework.

---

## Pose 1 — the bob. `answerRight`, about 0.9s.

A pleased, weighted-on-one-leg bob. Half of `Jump`: her feet stay on the floor.

| Beat | Frames | What moves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dip | 4 | Knees bend a little, chin dips, ears drop back. The anticipation, and the beat everybody leaves out |
| Up | 6 | Figure lifts, chest opens, head comes up and tilts. Eyes widen, the smile deepens. **Both arms swing up** |
| Sparks | at frame 10 | The three strokes pop out over three frames |
| Past it | 4 | Head goes about 12% too far. Ears arrive 2–3 frames late. **The forearms are still rising.** Tail whips, base then mid then tip |
| Settle | 12 | Squash 0.94 / 1.05, weight lands on one leg, blink on the landing. Tail stops last. Sparks fade |

- Line of action: a **C leaning back**. Open and pleased.
- One secondary action only: the blink. The sparks are the staging, not a
  second idea.
- Mochi's brows lift slightly. Maui's ears do the same job.

### The smile is `SayHi`'s smile, exactly

**Do not invent a happy face for this screen. Copy the one the file already
has.** `SayHi` is the reaction to a tap on her face, and it is the warmest
thing in the file. The bob borrows its numbers verbatim:

| Part | Value | Mochi | Maui |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Eyes | 138% | Yes | Yes (sx from 110 to 151.8) |
| Brows | up 7 | Yes | None to move |
| Mouth curve | one vertex drops to y 19, handles out to 13.15 | Yes | Has no such path |
| Mouth | *unchanged* | -- | Her omega smile, widened a touch to 122 / 130 |

**`SayHi` never opens the mouth.** That is the whole finding. Her smile is her
existing mouth line **reshaped into a deeper curve** -- `0-3149`, `0-3150` and
`0-3151` are vertex handles on that path, and moving them is what makes her
look pleased. Nothing is drawn on top of her face.

**A drawn-on grin was tried and it was creepy.** Two `laugh` shapes, a wide
open mouth with pink inside, fading in over each character's real mouth. It
tested well as a still and read as a mask in place of a face. Deleted. The
difference is the whole lesson here: *the same face smiling more* reads as
warmth; *a different mouth pasted over the face* reads as a puppet.

**Maui gets almost nothing from the face, and that is what `SayHi` gives her.**
Big eyes, a head tilt, and her own smile very slightly wider. Her good answer
is carried by the sparks, the lift and the arms, not by her mouth.

### The arms

Both arms swing up and out to about head height, and it is the one part of the
bob that is neither `SayHi`'s nor `Jump`'s.

| | Shoulder, at the peak | Forearm, at the peak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maui, arm-right | 136.45 to **180** | -8.21 to **30** |
| Maui, arm-left | 136.45 to **172** | -8.21 to **24** |
| Mochi, arm-right | 145.19 to **207** | -6.56 to **44** |
| Mochi, arm-left | 136.45 to **196** | -8.21 to **36** |

Four rules are doing the work in those numbers:

- **Never mirrored.** One shoulder goes higher than the other and arrives two
  frames later. Twinned arms read as a machine.
- **The forearms drag.** They start three frames after the shoulders and peak
  three frames after them, so the arm unfolds rather than swinging as one stick.
- **The angles are re-based, not copied.** Mochi's arm bones rest at different
  numbers from Maui's, so the same value gives her a T-pose. Each arm is its own
  rest plus its own delta, and each was checked on the character it belongs to.
- **Past about 190 on Maui the paws disappear behind her head**, which is where
  the ceiling came from. Found by looking, not by deciding.

## Pose 2 — the wince. `answerWrong`, about 1.0s.

| Beat | Frames | What moves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flinch | 4 | Head pulls back, shoulders come **up**, the whole figure shrinks a little. This is the compress, and it is what makes it a take rather than a face swap |
| Wince | 6 | `mouth-open` squashes wide and flat. Mochi: brows pull up and together, eyes squeeze. Maui: the **eyelids come down**, the whiskers droop, and a sweat drop appears |
| Hold | 18 | The face holds. This beat carries the whole pose |
| Release | 14 | Shoulders drop, face returns, one slow blink last of all |

**The two characters reach the same expression by completely different means,
and that was found by looking rather than planned.** Mochi has brows, so hers
is a brow pose. Maui has none, so his is an eyelid pose. Trying to give Maui
brows produced a cat wearing a girl's eyebrows, and it was deleted.

### Maui's wince, in detail

| What | How |
| --- | --- |
| Lid lines | Two new shapes, `lid-right` and `lid-left`, a thick dark bar sitting on the top of each eye. Opacity 0 at rest; they appear **only** in this pose. Tilted 8 degrees, inner end up |
| Half-lidded eyes | The eye path's **top vertex comes down** to y 2 and its handles widen to 7, so the top of the eye goes flat. The sides rise to y 4. The bottom does not move |
| Mouth | The `smile` node's **sy flips to -100**, turning the smile upside down into a frown. `mouth-open` stays hidden |
| Whiskers | `whiskers-left` and `whiskers-right` rotate down. **They are mirrored** -- the left rests at r 180 with a negative sy, so its droop is 166 while the right's is +14 |
| Sweat drop | A new teardrop shape on the **forehead**, fading in and drifting down |

**The bar over the eye is what finally sold it.** The half-lidded path on its
own was flat and unfeeling. A separate dark bar laid across the top of the eye
reads as a heavy lid, which is how sticker cats are drawn, and it is the one
thing that made him look sad rather than blank.

**Flipping the smile beats squashing a mouth open.** `mouth-open` widened to
420 was a straight bar and it read as neutral. The existing smile, turned
upside down, is a real frown and costs one keyed number. The `sy` crosses zero
on the way, so the mouth briefly vanishes -- over seven frames that reads as
the mouth turning down, not as a glitch.

**Squashing the eye's scale was tried first and is wrong.** Flattening `sy` to
45 makes two dashes, and two dashes read as *asleep*, not as wincing. Only
reshaping the path -- a flat top over a curved bottom -- gives the heavy-lidded
look. The reference for it is any "unimpressed cat" sticker: the whole
expression is in the upper lid.

**Brows on Maui are a closed question.** They were built, looked wrong, and
were deleted. Cats read through eyes, ears and whiskers. Do not try again
without a new reason.

- Line of action: a **C pulled back and in**, deliberately the opposite curve
  to the bob's, so the two never read as the same move at speed.
- No sparks, no colour, no sound.
- The expression travels: eyes first, then mouth, then shoulders. Not one key
  for the whole face.

---

## Deliberately not built

- **Teeth.** The reference grimace shows them and neither character has any. At
  this size a teeth bar is about three pixels and reads as a smudge. Build them
  only if the wince fails to land in the running app, and then only as a shape
  inside `mouth-open`.
- **Hands on hips.** A second reference showed it. The paws cannot carry it —
  see the rig table. If the "come on, you know this" read is wanted later, it
  has to come from the head and shoulders, not the arms.
- **A pool of variants.** One pose each until they are proven. Variation is the
  next thing to add, not part of the first pass.

---

## Wiring

Two new timelines and two new states on **Layer 1** of `State Machine 1`,
alongside `SayHi` and `Jump`.

| | Value |
| --- | --- |
| In from `Idle` | 80 ms |
| In from `IdleAfterHi` | 80 ms — `SayHi` already needs both, and a missed one is invisible until somebody taps her face first |
| Out to `Idle` | 200 ms, on exit time |
| Triggers | `answerRight`, `answerWrong` on the `Character` view model |

**No listeners, and the tap-overlap trap therefore does not apply here.** That
trap is about one finger landing on several shapes at once. These are fired
from Dart, one at a time, and the drill wraps her in an `IgnorePointer`
anyway.

## How to know it worked

- Captures at **88 pixels wide**, not at full size. A pose that only reads at
  512 has not been checked.
- Both characters, at the extreme frame of each pose, not at rest.
- The bob must not clip. Measured: `Jump` already lifts the `Group` 15 pixels
  (485 to 470) and her ears stay inside, so 15 is the proven headroom. The bob
  uses 9. **The artboard does not need to be taller** -- every screen fits the
  whole artboard into a box, so a taller one would shrink her app-wide to buy
  room for one small hop. The artboard also has clipping switched off, which is
  a safety net rather than something to lean on.
- `/breath-events` after the editor session, whatever was touched.
- Then the running app: seven answers in a row, and ask whether the fourth one
  is still welcome.

---

## What was actually built, 21 September 2026

| | |
| --- | --- |
| New shape | `sparks` -- one Shape, three stroke paths, `#3D5232` (the correct card's own green), 5px round caps, opacity 0 at rest |
| New timelines | `AnswerRight` 0.9s, `AnswerWrong` 1.0s. Both key **both** characters |
| New states | `AnswerRight`, `AnswerWrong` on Layer 1 of `State Machine 1` |
| New triggers | `answerRight`, `answerWrong` on the `Character` view model |
| Transitions | In from `Idle` and `IdleAfterHi` at 80 ms; out to `Idle` at 200 ms on exit time |

**Proven by simulation, not by eye:** `answerRight` from `Idle`, and
`answerWrong` from `IdleAfterHi` (reached through a face tap), both enter their
state and return to `Idle`.

**The breath events were already missing when this session opened the file, and
were repaired.** Nothing in this work went near the `Breathe` timeline. That is
the third recorded loss and it matches `breath-events`' own warning that any
session can lose them. Both keys are back and proven in the trace; whether the
version shipped before this one had them is unknown, so the app is worth
watching.

**Still to do.** The only proof of motion is the running app -- the editor MCP
renders static frames, so every pose here was judged by posing the statics,
capturing, and restoring. Two things need looking at on a device:

- Does the bob read at 88 pixels, or is it only the sparks doing the work? At
  that size the face change is close to invisible; the sparks and the lift are
  the message.
- Is the fourth one in a sitting still welcome, or already tiring?

---

## Revision, 21 September 2026 -- Maui's wince

Reported as "not as adorable and expressive as the girl's". It was true, and
the diagnosis was right: no brows, and a mouth that was not wide enough.

| Tried | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Give Maui brows | **Deleted.** A cat in a girl's eyebrows. They were even named `brow-left` / `brow-right`, colliding with Mochi's in the layer list |
| Flatten the eyes with `sy` | **Rejected.** Two dashes read as asleep |
| Reshape the eye path into a half-moon | **Kept.** This is the whole expression |
| Droop the whiskers | **Kept.** The cat-native equivalent of a brow |
| Widen `mouth-open` from 175 to 420 | **Replaced.** A wide bar reads neutral. Flipping the `smile` upside down gives a real frown |
| A dark bar laid over the top of each eye | **Kept.** This is what made him look sad rather than blank |
| Sweat drop in the top-left corner | **Moved to the forehead.** Out in the corner it belonged to nobody |
| Add a sweat drop | **Kept.** Parented inside Maui's `head`, so the skin swap hides it and Mochi never gets one |

**A mark belongs to a character when only that character should have it.** The
sparks sit on the artboard because both characters earn them. The sweat drop
sits inside Maui's head, because Mochi's wince already works without one. That
is also why it needed `sendToFront` -- a new child is added at the back, and
the drop was drawing behind his ear.

**The breath events were lost again during this session and repaired again.**
That is the fourth recorded loss. The check is one call and it has now caught
it twice in one day.

---

## A warning about captures

`capture_artboard` renders whatever the editor is currently showing, and for
most of this work that was **both characters at once** -- Mochi standing
behind Maui at full opacity, because the file's resting state has every
character switched on and the skin timelines are what hide them.

So Maui looked like he had a dark cap around his face. He does not. That was
Mochi's hair showing through his head's soft gradient. The moment the editor
previewed a skin timeline, the "cap" vanished and it looked like damage.

**Judge a character only in a capture where the other one is hidden**, or the
poses get tuned against a composite that never ships.

## The breath events, again

Lost and repaired twice more in this sitting -- five recorded losses now. The
check caught both. It is one call and it is not optional.

---

## Revision, 21 September 2026 -- the smile, twice

Asked for "a big open mouth smile" on the correct answer, then "almost like a
laugh, not just an oval", and then, on seeing it: **"the big smile is
creepy"**.

| Tried | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Scale `mouth-open` up | Rejected. Maui's is an Ellipse primitive, so every size of it is an oval |
| Two drawn `laugh` shapes, one per character | **Deleted. Creepy.** A grin laid over a face is a mask, not an expression |
| Copy `SayHi`'s numbers | **Kept.** The file already had the right smile |

**The rule this leaves behind: when a new expression is wanted, look for one
the file already performs before drawing anything.** `SayHi` had been sitting
there the whole time, and it took two rounds of new art to arrive at it.

**Names now carry the character.** `laugh-cat`, `lid-cat-right`,
`lid-cat-left`, `sweat-cat`. The first pass called the cat's new shapes
`brow-right` and `brow-left`, which collided with Mochi's real brows in the
layer list and read as though hers had been moved. Nothing of hers had been
touched, but the file looked like it had. **Name a new part for the character
it belongs to.**

---

## The breath events, tally

Six recorded losses now, three of them in this one sitting. Every loss was
caught by the same single call and repaired in one more. Not one of the
sessions that lost them went anywhere near the `Breathe` timeline.

**Run the check immediately before every export, and never export without it.**

---

## Revision, 21 September 2026 -- the arms

Asked for the arms and forearms to do something on a correct answer.

They swing up and out. The shoulders lead, the forearms drag three frames
behind, and nothing is mirrored. The heights differ per character because the
bone rests do: **re-base, never copy.** Maui's ceiling is about 190 on the
right shoulder, above which her paws vanish behind her head.

This is the one part of the bob borrowed from neither `SayHi` (one arm, a wave)
nor `Jump` (both arms, much bigger). It is deliberately about half of `Jump`.

---

## Revision, 21 September 2026 -- she is 180 tall now

Reported as: the expression cannot be seen. That was this brief's own
prediction, written at the top of it -- "at 88 pixels a facial expression is
nearly illegible" -- and it came true.

She sat in an **88 x 104** box beside the sentence. Beside a sentence there is
nowhere to grow: every point she takes comes off the words. So the layout
changed instead.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | Left of the bubble | Left of it, standing on the edge of the screen, the bubble lapping over her tail |
| Box | 88 x 104, `Fit.contain` | **140 x 180, `Fit.cover`** |
| Drawn | 88 x 88 | **180 x 180**, cropped to 140 wide |
| Head, ear to ear | 50 px | **103 px** |
| Bubble width, 375 | 243 | 229 |

**A row splits one width two ways, so she can only grow by taking points off
the words -- unless the points come from somewhere nothing was using.** Three
places do, and between them she doubled while the sentence gave up 14 points:

| Where from | Points |
| --- | --- |
| The empty margin inside her own square artboard, cropped off with `Fit.cover` | about 40 |
| The page gutter on her side, which she now stands out through | 16 to 24 |
| The end of her tail, which the bubble laps over | 10 |

**She is a figure inside a 500-unit square, not a figure the shape of one.**
Measured off the artboard: everything she has runs from x 78, her left
whiskers, to x 430, the tip of her tail. A square box therefore spends about
40 points on nothing. `Fit.cover` draws her 180 wide and the 140-point window
crops that margin off either side -- 8 points clear on her left, 5 on her
right. Narrower starts cutting, and her whiskers are the cat's brows.

**The bubble does not bleed. She does.** For one pass both of them ran out to
the screen edges, and a bubble touching the edge looked like it had fallen
off. She can stand on the edge; the sentence has to sit on the page.

The layouts this replaced, so none of them is tried again:

| Tried | Why it went |
| --- | --- |
| Beside her, both bleeding out to the screen edges | The bubble on the edge of the screen looked wrong, and it only reached 213 |
| Stacked under her, nothing overlapping | Cost 180 points of height -- on the fix step, the difference between three answers on the page and two |
| The sentence laid over her legs, full page width | 343 points wide, the widest of the lot, and not what was wanted: the bubble belongs beside her |

**180, and the iPhone SE decided it.** Taller and a sorting step's two answer
cards move below the fold on a 375 x 667 screen, and both answers being
visible at once is the one thing that step cannot give up.

## The finish step -- her head only

"Here it is." is the one screen in the drill where she is looking at something
the reader made, so her face is the whole point of her being there. A whole
standing figure 88 points wide put it at about 50 pixels.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Box | 88 x 104, whole figure | **190 x 150, head only** |
| Drawn | 88 x 88 | **250 x 250**, cropped |
| Head, ear to ear | 50 px | **142 px** |
| Where | Right of the bubble | **Above** it, right-aligned |
| Bubble tail | `right` | **`up`**, pointed at the middle of her head |
| Bubble width, 375 | 243 | **343** |

The crop is arithmetic on the artboard rather than a guess. Measured off a
500-unit capture: head top y 12, chin y 268, ears x 105 to 390, whiskers x 78
to 420. Drawing her at 250 and showing the top 190 x 150 of that lands the
window on x 60 to 440, y 0 to 300 -- ears, whiskers, face, and the top of the
collar, with 9 and 5 points to spare either side.

**Stacked, not beside.** A head that size and a bubble cannot share a row; one
would be paying for the other, and on this screen the reader's own sentence is
the thing that has to be easy to read. Stacked it gets the whole page, which
is where the 243 to 343 comes from.

`SkCharacter` gained `fit` and `alignment` for this, defaulting to what every
other screen was already doing. **A cropping fit needs a `ClipRect` around
it** -- the runtime paints outside its box otherwise.

**The finish step keeps the small box on purpose.** She is company for the
reader's own sentence there, with no pose to read. Big is for the seven
moments she is reacting.

**What this means for the poses.** The face is now worth about three times
what it was, so the bob's eyes and smile and the wince's lids and frown carry
real weight. The sparks are no longer doing the whole job. Nothing in the Rive
file changed; the poses simply became visible. Worth re-judging both at the
new size, and the wince first -- it was the one tuned hardest against an
illegible face.

## Revision, 22 September 2026 -- she is on every step now

She was on the six sorting steps, the fix and the finish. Nine of the drill's
fifteen steps had no character at all, so she walked on and off the lesson four
times, and the first criticism in it was said by somebody who had arrived one
step earlier.

The rule that kept her off the rest was **"a character with nothing to say is
Rive work for nothing"** -- the rule that put an orb on the tighten screen. It
is about **building poses**, and her idle is already in the file. It never
reached the question of whether she should simply be present, and reading it as
though it had is the scope fault `CLAUDE.md` ends on.

Two sizes now, and the size is the difference between talking and listening:

| Where | Box | Beside her |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The six sorting steps and the fix | 140 x 180 | The sentence, in a bubble |
| The finish | 150 x 200, centred | The reader's own sentence, under her |
| Everything else | 76 x 96 | The step's own heading |

Three rules came with it, and dropping any one brings back a version of the
fault. `test/swap_drill_view_test.dart` pins all three.

- **No bubble where she is quiet.** The introduction, the situation question,
  the three builder steps and the closing are the app talking. A bubble there
  would put the app's words in her mouth on the one part of the lesson that
  belongs to the reader.
- **No pose where she is quiet.** The bob and the wince are a reaction to a tap
  that was marked, and nothing on those steps is marked. The serial is still
  passed through unchanged, because a quiet step that reset it to zero would
  re-fire her bob the moment somebody stepped back on to an answered sentence.
- **The same box on every quiet step**, whatever the heading beside it is. She
  is pinned to the top of the row and the heading centres on her, so a two-line
  title and a one-line title leave her in the same place.

**96 is a presence rather than a performance.** This brief's own finding is
that a face this small is close to illegible -- which is the whole argument for
180 where she reacts, and no argument at all where there is no expression to
read.

**The finish step now shares the drill's one `SkCharacter`.** It built its own
until this change: a second decode of the file, which is the girl-then-cat
flash the sorting steps had already been fixed for.

## The girl-then-cat flash

Also reported: the character "switches from girl to cat suddenly".

`SkCharacter` already settles the `Skin` layer before its first paint, so a
cold open is correct. The drill was re-triggering that cold open on **every
step**: the step's scroll view is keyed by step index, so Continue threw the
whole subtree away and built a new one, and the Rive file decoded from scratch
seven times in a sitting.

Fixed by giving her a `GlobalKey` owned by `_SwapDrillViewState` and handing it
down through `_Step`. Flutter re-takes a global-keyed element in the same frame
it is removed, so the same character now crosses every step change. The file is
decoded once per drill.

**A character inside a keyed subtree needs a global key.** Anywhere else in the
app that keys a step and puts her inside it has the same bug waiting.

docs.title: Assertiveness practice
docs.body:
# Saying it out loud

The practice half of assertiveness. Not the beliefs -- those are already
written. This is the sentence you say, out loud, to a person who is pushing
back.

Built: the first lesson, "say it with I", at `/practice/say-i`. Drills A
and B and the seventeen remaining sentences are written here and not built.

| Thing | Where |
| --- | --- |
| How to write one | `.claude/skills/practice-writer/SKILL.md` |
| The app's own voice, which is **not** this one | `_docs/kind-writing-style.md` |
| The nineteen rights | `_docs/references/Assertiveness l _ your rights.pdf` |
| The techniques | `_docs/references/Assertiveness II.pdf` |
| The belief half, already written | `_docs/briefs/affirmation-explanations.md` |

## Why this exists

The 44 lines all answer a belief. Sheet I of the handout is the same shape:
nineteen rows, a rule swapped for a right.

**A right removes the reason not to. It does not supply the words.** Somebody
can agree they are allowed to say no and still have no sentence ready when it
is their turn to speak.

Sheet II supplies the sentence. Reading it does nothing either -- a technique
is a thing you say, in a voice, at normal volume, while somebody pushes back.

So the unit here is not a line you read. It is a line you say.

## What the reader never sees

The handout names its techniques: basic assertion, empathic assertion, broken
record. **None of those words reach the reader**, under rule 12. They are how
this file talks, not how the app does.

## One rule is bent on purpose

Rule 2 bans instructions -- "should", "try to", "remember to" -- because they
pile into a to-do list nobody asked for.

**"Say it out loud" is an instruction and it stays.** The difference is that
the reader opened a practice screen. An instruction inside a thing somebody
chose to do is the thing they chose. An instruction arriving on a lock screen
is not.

It is said once, plainly, and never repeated on the same screen.

## Spoken lines take contractions

The affirmation lines avoid them -- a line read at a glance is cleaner
without. These are read out loud, and "I would rather not" is not a sentence
anybody says.

Every spoken line here contracts.

---

# The rule under everything: say "I"
