Sheet II gives it straight: basic assertion uses "I" statements. It is the
most portable thing in the handout and it decides whether a sentence lands or
starts a row.

**A sentence about the other person puts them on the back foot.** They stop
hearing what happened and start defending who they are. Nothing after that
gets in.

| Points at | Example | Use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who they are | "You're so thoughtless." | Never |
| What they did | "When you leave it this late..." | Yes |
| You | "I didn't know about that." | Yes |
| The thing that happened | "That hurt." | Yes |

**The rule is not "never say you".** The handout's own example says "you" and
is right: *"When you leave it this late to produce your report..."* The word
is fine on a behaviour. It is the word on a character that starts the row.

Its step 1 says why in its own terms: describe the behaviour **without
interpreting or judging**. "Late" is a fact. "Thoughtless" is a verdict, and a
verdict is a thing to argue with.

Three words give it away nearly every time:

- **always** -- "You always leave it late."
- **never** -- "You never tell me."
- **so** -- "You're so difficult."

## This is not the app's rule reversed

Easy to misread later, so it is written down.

| Who is speaking | Which word | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The app, to the reader | "you" | Rule 1. Distance lowers how hard a feeling lands |
| The reader, to another person | "I" | Sheet II. It keeps the other person off the defensive |

Two speakers, two jobs. Neither cancels the other.

---

# The screen

Settled 20 September 2026, after an illustrated version was tried and
dropped.

## Illustrating the scenario does not work

Nineteen rights means nineteen-plus scenarios. Drawing each one means deciding
which feeling fits, nineteen times, and each decision can be wrong.

It is also the wrong target. **The scenario changes every time. The mechanism
never does.**

Two things are true in every drill:

1. Their words keep changing.
2. Your line does not.

## So the layout is the lesson

**Still true, and the arrangement below was superseded on 20 September 2026 --
see "Context comes before practice".** The rule survives; the stepped screen
it was first drawn for did not.

```
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │                               │
  │   "It's only two minutes."    │  theirs
  │                               │  new every time
  │                               │  arrives, then goes
  │   ─────────────────────────   │
  │                               │
  │   "No thanks,                 │  yours
  │    I'm not interested."       │  same words
  │                               │  same place, same size
  │   ─────────────────────────   │  never moves
  │                               │
  │            (her)              │  one idle pose
  │                               │
  └───────────────────────────────┘
```

Their line arrives and goes. Yours sits still, in the same box, at the same
size, from the first push to the last.

**The app already holds this rule.** On the breathing screen the sidekick must
never shift, because a thing that moves while you are matching it has moved on
you. Your sentence is the fixed thing here, for the same reason.

| | Per-scenario art | Your line not moving |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assets | Nineteen and counting | None |
| A judgement call each time | Yes | No |
| Teaches the skill | Sideways | Directly |
| Competes with speaking out loud | Yes | No |

## What the sidekick does

Nothing. One idle pose, below the lines.

She is not teaching and she is not the person pushing back. She is company,
which is what fixes the embarrassment. An illustration does not.

## Cloud, fire and wave are not cancelled

Shapes standing for a feeling were the right instinct in the wrong drill.
Here, the feeling is not the topic -- the sentence is.

They belong to the self-compassion lessons, where the feeling **is** the
topic. Kept for that, out of this.

## Rule 4 and pictures

Worth writing down, because somebody will raise it.

Rule 4 bans metaphors. A fire standing for heat is one.

It survives, narrowly, and only as a picture. Rule 4 exists because a
comparison in a *sentence* makes the reader hold two things and work out which
part was meant. That is a puzzle. A picture is read before words happen, so
there is nothing to work out.

**Show it, never say it.** The ban holds on every caption, every time.

---

## Context comes before practice, and the Next button is gone

Settled 20 September 2026, after the stepped version was built and looked at.

The first build handed the reader one sentence at a time behind a Next
button, and opened on the fourth line of the argument. Three faults, and they
are the same fault:

| What the reader got | What was missing |
| --- | --- |
| "Say \"you\", and they stop hearing what happened." | Any reason to be on this screen |
| A line, a button, a line, a button | Any idea how long it went on for |
| Two lines at a time | The shape -- theirs changing, yours not |

**The layout was the lesson and one sentence at a time could not show it.**
The whole point is that the "you" line keeps changing and the "I" line does
not. Two lines on a screen is the one arrangement where that is invisible.

So the page is read top to bottom, in groups:

```
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │            (her)              │  fixed, one idle pose
  │ ───────────────────────────── │
  │  Saying it out loud           │  what this is
  │  three short lines            │
  │                               │
  │  Today: saying it with "I"    │  the rule, and why
  │  two short paragraphs         │
  │                               │
  │  Pick one. Say the second     │  the one instruction
  │  line out loud.               │
  │                               │
  │  ▸ They let you down.         │  two situations
  │  ▸ Something wasn't fair.     │  one opens at a time
  │                               │
  │  The one that catches         │  the closer
  │  everybody                    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘
```

**Superseded again on 20 September 2026: the page is five chapters.**
`_docs/briefs/practice-tab-layout.md` holds the argument. The grouping above
survives untouched -- what went is the single scroll that held all five groups
at once, which is a wall on a phone. A forward control comes back, and the
piece behind it is a whole group rather than one sentence. **"Your turn" is one
chapter and may never be cut in two**, which is this section's rule restated.

**Two situations, two swaps inside each.** Four loose sentences in a row read
as a list to get through. A situation the reader picks is a thing that
happened to them, and the two lines under it are the same sentence said about
two different days. Open one and the other closes.

**Nothing is behind a press except the lines.** The reader scrolls; they do
not advance.

## The house voice is not this screen's voice

Settled 20 September 2026. The first build followed
`_docs/kind-writing-style.md` to the letter, and the screen came out with no
name for its own subject.

**That file was written for a different job.** It is the app talking to
somebody on a hard evening: a line on a lock screen, an empty state, an error
message, the account offer. Somebody in that position did not ask to be
taught, so a technique name is jargon, an instruction is a chore, and "we" is
a brochure claiming a togetherness the app has not earned.

**Somebody who opened a practice screen asked to be taught.** Everything
changes with that. A lesson that will not name its own subject teaches a trick
rather than a skill, and leaves the reader with nothing to look up, nothing to
recognise next time, and no idea what they just did.

So the rules split in two.

| Rule | On a lock screen | In a lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 -- never "we" | Holds. It claims a closeness the app has not got | Dropped. A teacher says "today we're practising" |
| 2 -- no instructions | Holds. They pile into a to-do list nobody asked for | Dropped. The instruction *is* the lesson |
| 12 -- no naming a technique | Holds. Jargon in front of somebody struggling | Dropped. The name is the thing being taught |
| 9 -- no promise | Holds, **and holds here**, hedged: "it can ease anxiety", never "it will" |
| 7 -- no claim about the reader | Holds, **and holds here**. The feeling is offered, never assumed |
| 15 -- nothing counts, always a way out | Holds, **and holds here**. No score, no tally, "That's enough for now" |

**The line between them is who asked.** A rule that protects somebody who did
not ask for this is kept. A rule that stops a teacher teaching is dropped.

`_docs/kind-writing-style.md` names the practice screens in its own scope
line, so this does not have to be rediscovered.

## Four parts, not two. The handout was read properly on 20 September 2026

The build before this taught **what happened** and **what you'd like**, with
the feeling offered as an optional extra. That is two of the handout's four
steps, and the missing one is the one that does the work.

Its **negative feelings assertion** is four steps, in order:

| Step | Its own wording | Its example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Describe the other person's behaviour objectively. Without interpreting or judging | *"When you leave it this late to produce your report..."* |
| 2 | Describe the impact on you. Be specific, don't overgeneralise | *"...it involves my working over the weekend..."* |
| 3 | Describe your feelings | *"...I feel annoyed about this..."* |
| 4 | State how you'd prefer it in future | *"...so in future I'd like to receive it by Friday lunch time"* |

**Step 2 was the one missing, and it is the one that makes a request land.**
"I've been sitting here an hour" is a fact nobody has to care about. "I've been
sitting here an hour and I've had to cancel my evening" is the same fact with a
cost attached. A request with no cost behind it is a preference.

Every scenario line was rewritten to carry a cost.

**Four steps are taught as optional on purpose.** Four parts read as a form to
fill in, and somebody who cannot manage all four says nothing at all. The
screen says so in the handout's own terms: two is a finished sentence, four is
the strongest one. Its other warning goes next to it -- *"Avoid unnecessary
padding and keep your statement simple and brief."*

## How a skill is actually taught, and what was missing

Skills training runs **instruction, modelling, rehearsal, feedback**. The build
before this did the first two and stopped.

| Stage | On the screen |
| --- | --- |
| Instruction | "Assertiveness" and "Today: the \"I\" sentence" |
| Modelling | "The shape of it" -- the four parts on one worked sentence |
| Rehearsal | "Your turn" -- the two situations, said out loud |
| Feedback | The app cannot hear anyone, so the handout's self-review stands in |

**The last section is the one a lesson usually drops, and it is three
paragraphs of the handout nearly word for word:**

- *"begin practising them in a neutral situation... where your emotions aren't
  too strong."*
- *"keep your voice calm, the volume normal, the pace even, keep good eye
  contact, and try and keep your physical tension low."*
- *"the first time you try these techniques they may not go the way you
  planned. It is important you don't beat yourself up about this but look at
  what went wrong and how you might do it differently next time. And then have
  another go! Over time you will find that they get easier."*

Without them, somebody practises on the argument they have been dreading, in a
shaky voice, and concludes they are bad at this. The words were taught and
nothing else.

**"It does get easier" is the one promise on the screen and it is the
handout's.** It is a claim about repetition, not about any conversation going
well. The price section of the handout is still to be built and still says
there is no guarantee of outcome.

## The voice is the handout's, not the app's

The user's note on the first rewrite: *"sounds not bad but can be more
conversational and natural."* Correct, and the reason is that the house voice
was still leaking through -- clipped declaratives, every sentence the same
length, no contractions where a person would use one.

The register to copy is the module's own. It writes *"By this we mean one where
your emotions aren't too strong"*, *"And then have another go!"*, *"Children
are experts at the broken record technique."* It is a person explaining
something, with asides.

So the screen contracts, uses asides, varies sentence length, and says the
awkward part out loud: *"It feels silly the first time. Everybody finds that."*

## What the page says now

> **Assertiveness**
>
> Assertiveness is asking for what you want without starting a row, and without
> going quiet either.
> It's a skill rather than a personality. Most people were never taught it, and
> it gets easier once you have the words.
> One thing worth knowing: saying how you feel out loud takes the edge off the
> anxiety. It's holding it in that keeps it going round.

> **Today: the "I" sentence**
>
> Here's the trouble with "you". Say "You always..." and the other person stops
> hearing what happened. They start defending who they are, and after that
> nothing you say gets through.
> So we turn it around. Instead of a verdict about them, you say what happened
> and what you'd like. There's nothing in that to argue with.
> It's the same thing you wanted. It's just about you now, instead of about
> them.

> **The shape of it**
>
> | Part | What it is for | Example |
> | --- | --- | --- |
> | When you... | What they did. Just the facts, no verdict | *When you come home late without telling me,* |
> | it means... | What it cost you. This is the part people leave out | *I end up worrying something's happened,* |
> | I feel... | How it left you. One word is plenty | *and it makes me angry.* |
> | I'd like... | What you actually want. Without this, it's just a complaint | *I'd really like a quick ring to say you're alright.* |
>
> The examples read straight down as one sentence.

> **Your turn**
>
> Pick whichever one sounds like your week. Say the second line out loud --
> actually out loud, not in your head. It feels silly the first time. Everybody
> finds that.

> **Before you try it on somebody**
>
> Start somewhere easy...
> Watch your voice as much as your words...
> The first go probably won't come out how you planned it...

Tests pin the structure rather than the wording: four frame steps in order, the
worked example reading as one sentence, "don't need all four" present, and the
practice section mentioning easy, voice and another go.

# Drill 0 -- swap the sentence

**The first lesson. Build this one.**

Every line in every other drill is an "I" sentence. Somebody who has not got
this yet will say the right words in the wrong shape and get a row instead of
an answer.

It is also the fastest win in the set. It changes nothing about what you want.
It changes only who the sentence is about.

## The introduction

**These are the words. Settled 21 September 2026.** Four paragraphs, before the
first sentence is shown.

> This lesson is about talking to the people closest to us: partners, family,
> friends.
>
> When something's bothering us, it's easy to start with "you": "You always...",
> "You never..." But "you" statements can sound like blame. The other person
> feels attacked, gets defensive, and stops listening.
>
> "I" statements say how you feel and what you prefer instead, which makes it
> easier for the other person to hear you.
>
> Next you'll see six sentences. For each one, decide: is it a criticism, or is
> it expressing yourself?

Each paragraph does one job, and the one it replaced did none of them:

| Paragraph | Job | What the reader could not do without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Names who is on the other end | Picture the conversation. A drill about "the other person" could be about a call centre |
| 2 | Names what goes wrong, as a chain | See why it fails. Attacked, then defensive, then not listening -- three steps, not an opinion |
| 3 | Names what to do instead | Know what is being taught. The old lead said "one kind" and "the other kind" and never said what either kind was |
| 4 | Sets the question | Answer it. The drill now asks in exactly these words |

**Paragraph 4 is the one that binds the screen.** The two option cards read
**"A criticism"** and **"Expressing myself"**, and the helper under every
sentence reads **"Is that a criticism, or is it expressing yourself?"** They
were worded three different ways before this. One question asked one way is the
same rule that governs the breathing cues: a reader following one instruction
must not be handed two near-copies of it. Rewording any of the three means
rewording all four.

**"Us" and "our" are allowed here and are not a slip.** The no-"we" rule is
about the app claiming closeness it has not earned -- a lock screen line, an
empty state. This is a lesson the reader opened, and a teacher's "us" is how
the subject gets introduced. See the scope table in `CLAUDE.md`.

**Naming "I statements" is allowed here for the same reason.** The
no-naming-a-technique rule is about somebody who did not ask. This reader is
here to learn the thing, and a name is what they recognise the next time they
meet it.

### The tension in paragraph 2, on purpose

It sorts by the **pronoun**. The drill then teaches that the pronoun is not the
test:

| Card | Says | Is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | "I feel like you're being selfish." | Opens with "I". Still a criticism |
| 6 | "I'd rather you asked me first." | Says "you". Not a criticism |

That is deliberate and it is how every handout does it. The simple rule gets
somebody moving; the cards correct it while they are paying attention, which is
worth more than a hedge nobody reads. See "The one that catches everybody" and
"This is not the app's rule reversed".

**It only breaks if the drill is shortened and those two cards are the ones
cut.** They are the correction. Six sentences without them teaches the pronoun
rule and nothing else.

## The screen it is built on

**Built 21 September 2026.** `lib/features/practice/views/swap_drill_view.dart`,
on its own route `/practice/swap`, with its own row in the practice list.

**It was a second screen rather than a sixth chapter of the reading lesson,
and on 21 September 2026 it became the only screen.** The lesson was a scroll
and this is a stepper -- two shapes wearing one name, teaching one subject,
on one tab. The stepper is the one that survived, because the point here is
the guess, and a guess needs one sentence at a time with nothing else to look
at. What the scroll had and this does not is listed in
`practice-tab-layout.md`, under the deleted chapter table.

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Top row | Back on the left, ✕ on the right. Fixed height; back is hidden on step one rather than removed |
| Progress bar | **One bar, filling once, continuous** |
| The step | Scrolls. Keyed by step, so each one arrives at the top |
| The pill | Full width, the theme's accent, **no arrow** |

**One bar, and no segments.** An earlier prototype ran two -- one for the six
sentences and one for the four builder steps -- and the second started empty,
which reads as starting again halfway through. Segments are worse than that:
thirteen ticks in a row is "3 of 13" drawn instead of written, and rule 15
bans the number either way. A test asserts progress only ever rises.

**No arrow beside the label.** The label says what pressing it does. A test
fails any forward label carrying one.

**The ground is a fixed off-white, `#F4F3EF`, in every theme.**
`lib/app/widgets/sk_exercise_colors.dart` holds the set and the reasons. Two
of them:

- An exercise should read the same on the sixth visit as on the first. A
  ground that goes warm in Coral diorama and cool in Dusk terrarium makes six
  different promises about the same lesson.
- A lesson is long-form reading, and off-white is the quietest ground text can
  sit on -- no hue to tint the ink, a fraction under white so it does not
  glare.

It is the same call the tighten screen made, the other way round: there the
orb is fixed and the page is the palette. Green and red are fixed too, because
they carry meaning and a theme that can recolour a wrong answer can lie about
it. The **accent** still paints the bar and the pill: two small marks of the
user's own palette on an otherwise neutral page.

`test/exercise_contrast_test.dart` asserts every pair clears 4.5:1. It carries
no audit baseline, unlike `contrast_test.dart` -- this ground is new, so there
is nothing to grandfather.

### The character says the sentences

**She holds each of the six in a speech bubble, and that is why she is on this
screen at all.** The plan was the opposite: an earlier build note had her
*removed* from the lesson for idling, which is the rule that took her off the
tighten screen -- a character with no job is Rive work for nothing. A sentence
in a bubble is a job.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Where | Top of the step, pinned to the top of a fixed 88×104 band |
| What moves | The bubble, downward. **She never does** |
| Which steps | The six sentences only |
| Taps | **Off.** `IgnorePointer` |

**The quote marks came off with the heading.** The sentence used to be a big
bold heading wrapped in quotes, which reads as the app's own words about the
reader. A bubble already says somebody said it.

**Not the introduction, not the rule, not the four builder steps.** Those are
the app teaching, and the reader building their own line. A bubble on either
would put words in the wrong mouth.

**Her reactions are off here, and that is the same call the lesson made.** The
two answer cards sit directly under her, and a thumb reaching past her for one
must not set her jumping mid-question.

**She is the one safe character in the app and she is now reading out "You
always keep me waiting."** The brief rejected making her the person pushing
back, on the grounds that being refused is the wrong job for her. Reading a
bad example aloud is not the same as meaning it, and the introduction labels
the six as examples before she says the first. If it ever starts to feel like
she is having a go at the reader, the fix is a second face for the examples,
not a smaller bubble.

## What the reader sees

> **What happens when you say "you"**
>
> They stop hearing what happened. They start defending who they are.
>
> Nothing you say after that gets in.

> **Say the second one out loud.**

> "You always keep me waiting."
>
> **"I've been sitting here an hour. I'd like to know if you're running
> late."**

> "You never tell me anything."
>
> **"I didn't know about that. I'd like to be told next time."**

> "You're being unfair."
>
> **"That doesn't seem fair to me. I'd like to talk about it."**

> "You made me look stupid."
>
> **"I didn't like how that went. I'd rather you asked me first."**

## Two parts: what happened, and what you'd like

**Superseded 20 September 2026 -- it is four parts.** See "Four parts, not
two" above. The section below is right about *why* the ask matters and wrong
about how many parts there are: it missed step 2, the cost to you, which is
the part that makes a request more than a preference.

A "you" sentence is short because it is a verdict, and a verdict needs no
second half. An "I" sentence has two.

| Part | Does what |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | Puts a fact down. Nothing to argue with |
| What you'd like | Makes it a request. Without it, it is only a complaint |

**The second half is the one people drop.** "I've been sitting here an hour"
on its own describes something. It asks for nothing, so nothing changes, and
next week the same thing happens and the sentence feels like it did not work.

The handout builds both parts into its longest technique: describe the
behaviour, then say what you would prefer in future. These are those two,
without the paperwork.

## The feeling is a third part, and it is optional

**Still true, and it is step 3 of four rather than an extra on the end.** The
handout lists it as a step in its own right. The screen offers it rather than
assuming it, for the reason below.

An early draft said "I'm fed up". That is a claim about the reader and the app
cannot know it -- rule 7, arriving inside a practice screen. Somebody who is
not fed up cannot say the line at all.

So it is offered, never assumed.

> "I've been sitting here an hour. I'm **annoyed**. I'd like to know if
> you're running late."
>
> annoyed / worried / hurt / tired / put out / embarrassed

**Two parts is a finished sentence.** Three is stronger. Neither has failed.

## The one that catches everybody

> "I feel like you're being selfish."
>
> That starts with "I". It still points at them. It does what a "you" sentence
> does.

> **The test is not the first word. It is who the sentence is about.**

## One word to keep out of the ask

"I'd like to be respected with my time" is the right shape and one word too
far. **Respected** says they disrespected you -- a verdict about them, wearing
an "I" on the front.

Say the thing you actually want instead. It is more concrete, and it is harder
to argue with.

| Verdict in the ask | The actual ask |
| --- | --- |
| "I'd like to be respected with my time." | "I'd like to know if you're running late." |
| "I'd like to be treated fairly." | "I'd like the same notice everyone else gets." |
| "I'd like some consideration." | "I'd like a text when plans change." |

## Why this is drilled and not just read

Nobody argues with it. Everybody agrees on the page, then says "you always"
the next time it matters, because that is the sentence that arrives first.

Saying the swapped version out loud four times is the part that sticks.

**The same rule binds the other seventeen.** A line supplies what happened and
what is wanted. The reader supplies anything the app cannot know.

---

# Drill A -- somebody selling something

Neutral on purpose. Sheet II says to practise first where the feelings are
small, and there is no relationship here to damage.

**This is the light one.** The biggest barrier to a speaking drill is not the
words, it is feeling silly saying them to a phone. Something light lowers
that, and this is the only drill where it is safe.

> **Your line**
> "No thanks, I'm not interested."
>
> Say it out loud now, once.

> **They say:** "It's only two minutes of your time."
>
> **You say:** "No thanks, I'm not interested."

> **They say:** "It's really more like ninety seconds."
>
> **You say:** "No thanks, I'm not interested."

> **They say:** "Could I speak to the homeowner?"
>
> **You say:** "No thanks, I'm not interested."

> **They say:** "Could I call you back on Sunday?"
>
> **You say:** "No thanks, I'm not interested."

> Four times. The same words. Nothing added.
>
> That is the whole thing.

## The joke is the gap, not the caller

They escalate. You do not move. That gap is funny, and it is also exactly the
skill.

**Nothing mocks the person pushing.** The handout's own sentence is *"I won't
allow you to take advantage of me and I won't attack you for being who you
are."* An app that sneers at the caller has taught contempt, which is the
thing being trained out.

So: funny about the situation. Never about a person. Never about the reader.

---

# Drill B -- a friend, and you want the evening in

Harder, because there is something to lose. It comes after the easy one, never
before.

**This one is straight.** *"Come for just an hour"* is the thing that actually
happens to people. A joke here says it does not matter.

> **Your line**
> "I'd rather not tonight."
>
> Say it out loud now, once.

> **They say:** "Come for just an hour."
>
> **You say:** "I'd rather not tonight."

> **They say:** "You always say that."
>
> **You say:** "I'd love to see you. I'd rather not tonight."

> **They say:** "Alright."

> The warm bit is allowed on the third go. The line after it does not change.

## Three decisions inside it

**The warm prefix is in the handout.** Its own example does the same -- the
third reply is "I am your friend, but I can't lend you any money." Holding one
line for three rounds with nothing warm in it reads as cold, and a technique
people feel cold using is one they stop using.

**The handout's "but" is not copied.** It warns about "but" on the same page
that it uses one. A full stop does the same job and takes nothing back, so the
line is "I'd love to see you. I'd rather not tonight."

**The last push is not a win.** "Alright" is somebody backing off, not
somebody pleased. Ending on agreement would teach that holding a line makes
people happy, and often it does not.

---

# The nineteen sentences

Two written. Seventeen to go, in the same shape.

## Right 13 -- you can say no

> **You can say no, and leave it at that.**
>
> **The rule you were given**
> Always fit in with people. If you do not, they will not be there later.
>
> **What you say**
> "I'd rather not."
>
> **What you leave off**
> The reason. "I'd rather not, because I'm tired" hands them something to
> argue with. Most people will. *"You could come for just an hour."*
>
> **Somewhere easy to start**
> A caller selling something. A sign-up in the street. Somebody you will never
> see again.

Other sentences that do the same job: "No thanks." / "I can't make it." /
"Not this time."

## Right 10 -- you can say it hurt

> **Saying that something hurt is allowed.**
>
> **The rule you were given**
> People do not want to hear that you feel bad, so keep it in.
>
> **What you say**
> "That hurt."
>
> **What you leave off**
> Two things. The bit that takes it back -- "that hurt, but I know you didn't
> mean it" -- because the second half cancels the first and it is the half
> they hear. And the bit about them. "That hurt" says what happened. "You're
> so thoughtless" says what they are, and nothing after it gets heard.
>
> **Somewhere easy to start**
> Out loud, on your own, about something that already happened. Nobody has to
> be in the room the first time.

Other sentences that do the same job, all of them on you or on the thing that
happened: "I didn't like that." / "That one stung." / "I feel hurt."

## Where the "leave it off" rule comes from

Sheet II makes the point twice, and it is the most useful thing in it:

- A statement is **brief and specific**. Padding is what makes it soft enough
  to ignore.
- A "but" in the middle **devalues everything before it**. Its example is "I
  appreciate your feelings, but...", which it calls aggression in a polite
  word.

The explanation for line 13 found the same thing from the other side: the
reason is what people argue with.

---

# The price is said out loud too

Sheet II has a section most training skips.

> Friends and family may have benefited from you being passive, and may
> sabotage your new assertiveness.
>
> You are reshaping beliefs you have held since childhood, and this can be
> frightening.
>
> There is no guarantee of outcome.

**Keep it.** An app that teaches saying no, and never says it can cost you
something, is wrong the first time it costs somebody something. Rule 9 bans
promises the app cannot keep, and "this will go well" is one.

In the house voice it is about three sentences, and it belongs at the start of
the whole thing, not at the end.

---

# Settled

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Illustrate each scenario? | No. Nineteen judgement calls, all of them able to be wrong |
| What is the visual? | The layout. Their line moves, yours does not |
| Cloud, fire, wave? | Not here. They belong to the self-compassion lessons |
| Can it be funny? | In Drill A only, about the situation, never about a person |
| Who pushes back? | Plain text. Not the sidekick -- she is not the one refusing you |
| Does anything count? | No. No score, no tally, rule 15 holds |
| How many parts? | Four, taught as optional. Two is a finished sentence |
| Teach how to practise? | Yes. Start easy, mind the voice, expect a bad first go |
| One line at a time? | No. Grouped. A Next button hid the shape because one sentence is too small to hold one |
| One page or chapters? | Five chapters, one group each. See `practice-tab-layout.md` |
| Name the technique? | Yes. A lesson names its subject. The house voice is for elsewhere |

# Open

- **The app cannot hear you.** Everything is written assuming a tap to move
  on. The mic could confirm somebody spoke without storing a word, which is a
  better gate and a real build. Not needed to find out whether the shape
  works.
- **Seventeen sentences to write**, now Drill 0 is built.
- **No voice on this screen.** The reference layout this was built from has a
  speaker button inside the bubble, and `assets/audio/` holds the panic screen
  and nothing else. A speaker that plays nothing is worse than no speaker, so
  the spot is left empty rather than filled with a dead control. Worth doing
  the day the voice work reaches the lessons -- the words are already one
  string per line, which is the shape a recording needs.
- **The sentence the reader builds is gone when they close the page.** Either
  that is accepted, or this one screen keeps a draft. A real decision about
  the "nothing is saved" rule, not a detail.
- **Where this lives.** `/practice/swap`, one row on the Practice tab, under a
  "Communication skills" heading.
- ~~**The "you" paragraph is now written twice.**~~ Answered 21 September
  2026: the reading lesson was deleted, so it is written once, on page 2 of
  the drill's introduction.
- ~~**Three things from the deleted lesson are not on any screen.**~~ Closed
  21 September 2026, the same day it opened. The trap was already card three.
  "Before you try it on somebody" became a new last step -- three paragraphs:
  start easy, watch your voice, expect a bad first go -- so the drill no
  longer ends on the reader's sentence, it ends on how to use it. "It's a
  skill rather than a personality" was tried on introduction page one and
  taken back out; `practice-tab-layout.md` holds why, and "it does get easier"
  on the closing step is where that idea lives now.
- **The drill is now seven minutes and length is its failure mode.** It has
  grown three times in one day: four introduction pages, a relabelled finish,
  and a closing page. **The next addition should take something out.** The
  opening page and the situation step are the candidates. The six sentences,
  the fix, the builder and the closing are the clinical parts and are not.

# Sources

- `_docs/references/Assertiveness l _ your rights.pdf` -- the nineteen rights.
- `_docs/references/Assertiveness II.pdf` -- the verbal and non-verbal
  characteristics, the six techniques, the payoffs and the price.
- `_docs/kind-writing-style.md` -- the voice.
- `_docs/briefs/affirmation-explanations.md` -- the belief half.
- "I" statements are Thomas Gordon, *Parent Effectiveness Training* (1970),
  who coined the I-message and the you-message. Studies putting the two side
  by side find a "you" sentence draws more anger than an "I" sentence about
  the same event. The working part is **blame, not the pronoun** -- "I feel
  like you're being selfish" is a you-sentence with an I on the front and gets
  the same reaction. Gottman's work on how a row starts is the nearest famous
  relative and is not the source.
- **No name reaches the reader.** Rule 12 bans naming a theory or a
  researcher, rule 13 bans famous names. If a resources page is ever wanted,
  the Centre for Clinical Interventions is free, publicly funded, has its own
  assertiveness module, and is already cited in these briefs. Not the Gottman
  Institute -- it sells courses, and the end of a hard evening is not
  somewhere to hand somebody a shop.

docs.title: Breath event fixed
docs.body:
Done. I did not touch the Rive file. Here is what I found.

Why the editor deleted the keys

- The two keyframes were written directly into the file data by the MCP tools, on the trigger's fire property (key 869).
- The Rive editor has no screen for this kind of keyframe. It cannot show it, list it, or read it back (_docs/handoff.md:105-114 records this).
- When you edit that timeline, the editor rewrites the timeline from what it knows. It does not know about those two keys. So it saves the timeline without them.
- So it is not a random bug. It is: we stored data the editor cannot see, and the editor is the thing that saves the file. This will happen on every edit. We cannot fix the editor.

Does exporting for Flutter help?

- Partly, and you already have this. assets/rive/character.riv is the export, and it is in git. That copy is safe. The keys only die in the source file in the cloud editor, and the loss only reaches the app on the next export.
- So export does not fix the cause. It only means an old good export can be restored from git.

Two real fixes:

Option 1 — Use Rive Events instead of keyed triggers (recommended)

- A Rive "Event" is a named marker you place on a timeline, like a flag on frame 0 and frame 186. Events are a normal editor feature. The editor shows them on the timeline, so they survive editing, and you can see with your own eyes that they exist.
- The Flutter runtime reports events when the playhead passes them. Your rive: ^0.15.0-dev.1 package supports an event listener on the state machine, and the app already plays Breathe through a state machine, so this fits.
- Change needed: add two events in the editor, and swap ~10 lines in lib/app/widgets/sk_character.dart from view-model trigger listeners to an event listener.
- One risk: an old bug report (issue #591 (https://github.com/rive-app/rive-flutter/issues/591)) says listeners did not fire in version 0.14.0. So we still verify once on the simulator. But after that, the "re-add before every export" rule dies, because the editor protects events itself.

Option 2 — Keep the current design

- Keep the re-add rule: after any editor session, re-key fire (869) at frames 0 and 186, export, and watch the counter on the simulator.
- Cost: a manual, un-checkable step forever, and it multiplies if you add more characters or timelines.

My recommendation: Option 1. It moves the two markers from a place the editor cannot see into a place it can. When your current animation work is done, I can build and verify it.

Sources: Rive Events overview (https://rive.app/docs/editor/events/overview), rive_native StateMachine API (https://pub.dev/documentation/rive_native/latest/rive_native/StateMachine-class.html), rive-flutter issue #591 (https://github.com/rive-app/rive-flutter/issues/591)

✻ Baked for 2m 5s · 1 shell still running

❯ ok before u do so, is this a large task

No. It is a small task.

The steps and their size:

1. Add two events in the Rive editor on the Breathe timeline — minutes.
2. Change ~10–30 lines in lib/app/widgets/sk_character.dart — swap the trigger listeners for one event listener — small.
3. Re-export, copy to assets/rive/character.riv — minutes.
4. Run the app on the simulator and watch the counter reach "Breath 2 of 2" — this is the longest step, maybe 15–20 minutes. It is the same QA you must do today anyway.
5. Update the notes in CLAUDE.md and the code comments — small.

Total: under an hour, and most of it is the QA we already owe on any Rive change.

The one real risk: the event listener may not fire in your rive 0.15.0-dev.1 package (there was a bug like that in 0.14.0). We find out in step 4. If it fails, we revert — the old working file and code are in git, so the cost of a failed try is small.

✻ Baked for 9s · 1 shell still running

※ recap: We're planning to replace the fragile breathing trigger keyframes with Rive Events so editor sessions stop deleting them. It's a small task, under an hour. Next action: you finish your current Rive edits, then tell me to start.

❯ ok let's try it. i just make some edits , should we commit and push changes before trying this small task? pls read handoff on some edits i just did in a separate terminal HANDOFF — Rive character tap fix (14 Sep 2026, session on branch track-rive-source)

  What was done
  - In the Rive cloud file "character" (editor.rive.app/file/character/2576025):
    - Renamed animation + state "EarTwitch" -> "Jump" (the whole-body reaction).
    - Swapped the two tap listeners: body now fires tapEar -> Jump, face now
      fires tapTorso -> SayHi. (They were reversed vs. the intended design:
      tummy = jump, face = say hi.)
    - Second bug found via Rive's simulateStateMachine: hit areas overlap, so a
      face tap fires tapTorso AND tapEar in the same frame, and transition
      evaluation order (creation order, invisible in the editor) let Jump win.
      Fixed by swapping the CONTENTS of existing transitions so SayHi and the
      ear twitches are evaluated before the catch-all Jump. Verified in the
      simulator from both Idle and IdleAfterHi.
    - Re-added the inhale/exhale trigger keyframes on the Breathe timeline
      (fire key 869, frames 0 and 186, hold) before export, per CLAUDE.md rule.
  - Exported and copied to assets/rive/character.riv.

  Uncommitted changes in the working tree (nothing committed yet)
  - assets/rive/character.riv  (new export)
  - lib/app/widgets/sk_character.dart  (comment block updated to new behaviour)
  - CLAUDE.md  (new section: taps hit every overlapping shape; transition order
    picks the winner; any new tap reaction must be proven with a two-trigger
    simulateStateMachine run from Idle AND IdleAfterHi)

  Still open / gotchas for the next task
  - Simulator QA not yet confirmed by the user: face -> SayHi (twice in a row),
    tummy -> Jump, ear -> twitch, and panic breathing counter reaching
    "Breath 2 of 2". Needs a full app restart, not hot reload.
  - Trigger names are stale ON PURPOSE: face fires tapTorso, everything else
    fires tapEar. Read a listener's target, not its trigger name. Renaming
    was deliberately skipped as too risky this session.
  - MCP tool limits hit this session: delete_objects is permission-blocked in
    auto mode; transitionorder (key 159) and sourcepathids (key 588) are
    unsettable types. Workaround used: set_property_values on statetoid (151) /
    targetid (224) and animation_editor updateConditions.
  - export_file cannot write to disk directly (sandbox); use the curl/python
    recipe it returns, PLUS a notifications/initialized call after initialize
    or tools/call is rejected.
  - Standing rule unchanged: any Rive editor session must re-add the two
    breathe trigger keys before every export, then QA on the simulator.

Commit yes — but test first, push after. The handoff says the simulator QA was never done. A commit that says "tap fix works" with no proof breaks the project's own rule: the only proof is the running app. And my events task will touch the same file and the same widget, so we want a clean, proven checkpoint before I start.

The order:

1. Run the app on the simulator now — this QA was owed anyway.
2. You tap: face twice (SayHi both times), tummy (Jump), ear (twitch).
3. I check the breathing counter reaches "Breath 2 of 2" via screenshots when you open the panic button.
4. If all pass: commit and push. That is our safe point.
5. Then I do the events task.

I will start the app now.

  Ran 3 shell commands

The app is building on the iPhone 17 simulator. I will tell you when it is up.

While it builds, here is the test list for you:

1. Tap the face — she says hi.
2. Tap the face again — she says hi again (this was the double-tap bug).
3. Tap the tummy — she jumps.
4. Tap the ear — the ear twitches.
5. Then press the panic button. I will screenshot the breathing screen and check the counter reaches "Breath 2 of 2" myself.

One note from the handoff: this is a fresh app start, not hot reload, so the test is valid.

✻ Cooked for 52s · 1 shell still running

⏺ Background command "Wait for the app to launch or fail" completed (exit code 0)

  Read 2 files, ran 1 shell command

⏺ Monitor(Breath trigger firings (RIVEDIAG) and errors from the running app)
Monitor started · task by6hlrnmk · timeout 1800s

Please do these taps on the simulator, in order:

1. Tap her face — she should say hi.
2. Tap her face again — she should say hi again.
3. Tap her tummy — she should jump.
4. Tap an ear — it should twitch.
5. Press the orange panic button and stay on the breathing screen for about 40 seconds. Do not tap anything there.

I am watching the app's log while you do this. The code prints a line every time a breath trigger fires, so step 5 proves the counter without you reading the screen. Tell me what you saw for steps 1–4 (or if anything looked wrong), and I will check the log for step 5.

✻ Sautéed for 26s · 1 shell still running

❯ i did a qa and the tap interactions for face tummy ears work

Good — taps pass. Now I check the breathing triggers in the log.

  Searched for 2 patterns


The taps work, but breathing isn't confirmed—you visited /panic and /panic/body, yet no trigger print lines showed up, so either you left too early or triggers are broken in this export. I'll check the route names next to figure out which.

  Searched for 1 pattern

Found it. The breathing screen was never opened. The routes tell the story:

- /panic — the feeling picker
- /panic/body — the "What's happening in your body?" question
- /panic/breathe — the breathing pacer. This one never appears in the log.

You visited the picker and the body question, then went home. The trigger test needs the pacer itself.

One more step, please:

1. Get to the breathing screen — from the body question, tap a tile or "Skip this". You should see her pacing with "In through your nose."
2. Stay there about 45 seconds, no tapping. The lead-in takes ~11 seconds, then each breath is 10.

My log watcher is still on. The moment a breath trigger fires, I get told. If nothing fires after your 45 seconds, the export is broken and we know before committing.

docs.title: Communication lesson structure
docs.body:
# The shape of a communication lesson

Written 23 September 2026, against `/lesson-design`. **Both changes below are
built.** It is the skeleton every
lesson under **Communication skills** follows, and the audit of the one that
exists -- "When something's bothering you", `Routes.swapDrill`.

`/practice-writer` decides what a lesson says. This decides the order it is
said in and what goes on one screen.

---

## The skeleton

Twelve kinds of screen, in four parts. A lesson uses all four parts; the
number of screens inside part 3 is the only thing that varies.

| Part | # | Screen | The one thing it does | Rule behind it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learn** | 1 | The idea | Names the subject and says what it is good for | practice-writer 2 |
| | 2 | What goes wrong | The move everybody makes, and the chain it sets off | one subject a screen |
| | 3 | What to do instead | The replacement, on one line | practice-writer 5 |
| | 4 | The swap | One situation, said both ways, side by side | lesson-design 3 |
| **Spot it** | 5 | Sort a sentence | One sentence, one question | rehearse |
| | .. | (repeated) | Each one a different giveaway | |
| | 6 | Catch the trap | The failure case, as a question rather than a footnote | practice-writer 7 |
| | 7 | How it went | Feedback, inside one sitting, never stored | practice-writer 3 |
| **Say it** | 8 | Pick your own | The reader's own situation | |
| | 9 | The shape | The parts of the sentence, **immediately before** they are used | |
| | 10 | Build it | One part a screen | rehearse |
| | 11 | Your line | The whole sentence, and the invitation to say it out loud | practice-writer 6 |
| **Take it away** | 12 | Before you try it | Start easy, mind your voice, expect a rough first go | practice-writer 8 |

### Why four parts and not three

Skills training is **instruct, model, rehearse, feedback**. Learn is
instruct and model. Spot it is rehearsal of *recognition* -- can you tell the
difference in somebody else's sentence. Say it is rehearsal of *production* --
can you make one of your own. They are different skills and the second one
fails without the first.

### The stages are already named, and not by a label on the screen

The forward control changes word at every boundary: Continue, Start, Next
sentence, Pick one, Next, See it, One last thing. **That is the stage marker,
and it is enough.** A kicker over each heading saying "Part 2 of 4" was
considered and rejected twice over: it is a second thing to read on every
screen, and it is a count.

**The beat labels added on 23 September 2026 are not that, and the difference
is what each one names.** A kicker names where the reader is in the lesson,
which is a position in a sequence and a thing to keep track of. A beat label
names what the block under it holds. One is a count; the other is a signpost
to something on the same screen.

---

## The rules this shape is built on

Each is `/lesson-design`, applied. The skill holds the evidence.

1. **One subject a screen.** If the answer to "what does this screen teach?"
   needs an "and", it is two screens.
2. **About six lines of body text.** A list or a worked example is not body
   text and does not count against it.
3. **The reader presses on.** Nothing advances itself.
4. **A thing is taught where it is used**, never three screens early. This
   repo already made that call once -- the builder's one-line helpers were
   moved off the teaching page and on to the step that asks for the part.
5. **Nothing everybody needs goes behind a tap.** No accordion, no info icon,
   no "show more" on a teaching point, a model line, or the reason to carry
   on.
6. **One heading and at most one bold phrase a screen.**
7. **Cut what is not the point.** Interesting, true and related still costs
   the reader something. The test is: take it out, can the lesson still be
   taught?

---

## Inside one screen: situation, behaviour, impact

Chosen 23 September 2026. The skeleton above decides the **order of the
screens**. This decides the **order of the blocks inside one of them**.

SBI -- situation, behaviour, impact -- is the frame communication training
already uses to describe an exchange. It was picked over STAR (situation,
task, action, result), which was the first candidate and lost on one fact:
STAR is a frame for telling a story about something **you did**, and a
teaching screen is not a story about the reader. It shows a move and one
example of it. STAR's "task" and "result" have nothing to attach to, and
filling them in makes the page longer -- which is this lesson's failure mode.

The frame was found by reading "The trouble with 'you'" and naming what was
already on it, which is the argument for keeping it: it describes work that
already reads well, rather than a shape pushed on to it.

| Beat | What it holds | On "The trouble with 'you'" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Situation** | The everyday moment. One sentence, no example yet | "Say you're having dinner together, and the phone comes out again." |
| **Behaviour** | One example sentence, in a bubble, labelled with its kind | "You're always on your phone." |
| **Impact** | What it does to the other person, then the cost to the reader | Attacked, defensive, stops listening -- and the thing never gets talked about |

### The beats are on the screen, in the reader's own words

Decided 23 September 2026, and it is the half of this section that nearly did
not happen. The frame ran for one afternoon as an **authoring rule only** --
the blocks in the right order, nothing on the page saying so -- and that is
not enough. A page of five paragraphs is read as five paragraphs however well
it is ordered.

Each beat now carries a small label over the group it names. `SwapIntroBeat`
is the block; `_Beat` draws it, 13/600 uppercase in the exercise set's own
caption colour.

| Beat | Page 2 | Page 3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situation | ONE EVENING | SAME EVENING |
| Behaviour | WHAT WE SAY | WHAT TO SAY INSTEAD |
| Impact | WHAT HAPPENS NEXT | WHAT HAPPENS NEXT |

**The labels are never the frame's own words.** "SITUATION", "BEHAVIOUR" and
"IMPACT" were drafted first and rejected on `/practice-writer` rule 10: the
design word and the screen word are usually different, and only one of them
ships. Two of the three are abstract nouns, on a page read by somebody
learning something new on a bad evening. A label names what happens.

**The last row being identical is the point.** Same situation, same kind of
consequence, one thing changed between them -- that is what makes the two
pages a pair rather than two pages about one evening. A test pins it.

**They are not headings, and `/lesson-design` rule 5 still holds.** The page
has one heading, at 24/600, and it is still the only thing at that size. These
sit a step *below* body text. They are also not `Semantics(header: true)`:
three per page would bury the one real heading in a list of six.

### Which screens it governs

Screens 2 and 3 run all three beats. They are the two that **describe an
exchange**.

**Screen 4, the swap, carries situation and behaviour only, and that is
right.** It was written into this section as a third SBI page and checked on
23 September 2026: it does not need an impact beat, because screen 3 already
ends on one -- "It's the same thing you wanted. It's just about you now,
instead of about them." An impact line on screen 4 would be that sentence
again, and rule 7 above cuts it. **Screen 4's subject is the move, shown side
by side. The impact of each half is the two pages before it.**

It does not reach the rest at all:

| Screen | Why not |
| --- | --- |
| 1, the idea | Names the subject. There is no exchange on it yet |
| 5 to 7, the drill | The reader is answering, not being shown |
| 8 to 11, the builder | The reader's own situation, and the three-part sentence is the frame there |
| 12, before you try it | Advice about practising, not about one exchange |

**Where it does not apply, say so and leave the beat out.** A thin invented
situation on the top of a screen is worse than no situation, and it costs the
reader a line either way.

### The order never flips, and an exception was written here and withdrawn

For one afternoon on 23 September 2026 this section said **"impact first is
allowed on a page that replies to the page before it"**, because "What 'I'
does instead" opened on "there's nothing in it to argue with" and showed the
example after it.

That was not a rule. It was a description of a page that had no situation on
it, written up as though it had been chosen. Putting the labels on the screen
is what exposed it: an IMPACT label over the first block and a BEHAVIOUR label
under it reads backwards, and no wording fixes that.

Page 3 now opens on SAME EVENING like page 2, and the three run in order on
both. **Both pages run the same way twice. That is what makes them a pair.**

Worth keeping as a warning: a shape that is merely *what the page already did*
will pass for a decision if you write it down in the same voice as one.

### What it does not change

The seven rules above still bind. SBI says what the blocks are, not how many.
One subject a screen, about six lines of body text, one heading, at most one
bold phrase. A three-beat frame that pushes a page past those is the frame
being used wrongly.

---

## The audit: "When something's bothering you"

Eighteen steps today. Two of them carry two subjects, one thing is taught
three screens before it is used, and one teaching page has no situation on it.
Everything else passes.

**The third of those was found on 23 September 2026**, by running the frame
above over the lesson. The first two were found by reading the screens. Both
passes were worth doing, and they found different faults.

| Step | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| Intro 1 -- `"I" statements` | **Two subjects.** What the lesson is, *and* why it helps the anxiety |
| Intro 2 -- The trouble with "you" | **No situation.** It opened on the habit and went straight to the example. Change 3 |
| Intro 3 -- What "I" does instead | Passes |
| Intro 4 -- The swap | **Two subjects.** The three-part shape, *and* the same evening said both ways |
| Six sorting cards | Passes. Repetition is the point of a recognition drill |
| Fix one | Passes |
| Score | Passes. Feedback, one sitting, nothing stored |
| Situation | Passes |
| Three builder steps | Passes -- and see the trap below |
| Your sentence | Passes |
| Before you try it | Passes. Three headings, two points each |

### Change 1 -- the anxiety note moves to the closing

"Saying how you feel out loud takes the edge off the anxiety. It's holding it
in that keeps it going round."

It is on page one, in the **Worth knowing** box, as the reason to carry on. It
is the second subject on that page.

**It moves to `Before you try it`.** The trade is real and is written down
rather than discovered later: on page one it is a reason to keep reading; at
the end it is a reason to actually use the thing, and it lands beside "start
somewhere easy" where the reader is deciding whether to try it on a person.
The second job is the one worth having.

The box stays a box. The tone is `info`: worth knowing, no verdict.

**It is not folded into an accordion.** Everybody should read it, and
collapsed text cannot be scanned.

### Change 2 -- the three-part shape moves to just before the builder

Intro page 4 teaches two things: the three parts of the sentence, and the
before-and-after swap. The swap is that page's subject. The parts are used
three screens later, after the sorting drill and the situation picker.

**The parts get their own screen, directly after "Pick one" and directly
before the first builder step.** An instruction is worth most at the moment it
is followed -- which is the same argument that moved the per-part helpers off
this page on 21 September 2026. This is the other half of that decision,
finished.

Page 4 keeps the swap, and is one subject again.

Cost: one more screen. Eighteen steps becomes nineteen. Page 4 loses a block
but keeps its step, so nothing is saved back.

---

### Change 3 -- "The trouble with 'you'" gets its situation -- **built**

Applied 23 September 2026, when SBI was first run over the lesson.

The page opened on the **habit** -- "When something's bothering us, it's easy
to start with 'you'" -- and went straight to the example sentence. There was
no scene. Two things were wrong because of it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| The example | "You're always on your phone." arrived with nowhere to happen |
| Page 4 | "Same evening, said both ways:" pointed back at an evening nobody had been shown |

It now opens "Say you're having dinner together, and the phone comes out
again." The line after it lost its "When something's bothering us," -- the
scene says that now, and saying it twice cost a line.

**The page is about seven lines of body text rather than six.** That is over
rule 2 and it is the trade: a concrete scene is the strongest thing the frame
asks for, and the chain under it is a list, which does not count. The next
addition to that page has to take something out.

`test/swap_drill_script_test.dart` pins the order and not the words: prose
before the example, prose after it.

### Change 4 -- the beats go on the screen -- **built**

Applied 23 September 2026, the same day, after Change 3. The frame was
invisible: correct block order, nothing saying so.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Added | `SwapIntroBeat`, a small-capitals label over the group it names |
| Pages | 2 and 3. Page 4 has none -- its bubbles already carry two labels |
| Words | The reader's, never the frame's. See the section above |
| Also | Page 3 reordered to situation first, and the "impact first" exception withdrawn |
| Also | "It sounds like blame, and then:" lost its colon -- the label points at the chain now |

`test/swap_drill_script_test.dart` pins four things: three beats a page in
order, the same last label on both pages, none on page 4, and no label that
runs to a sentence. `test/swap_drill_view_test.dart` checks each one reaches
the screen upper-cased, and the existing 200% pass on the SE still holds.

---

## What was checked and left alone

**The three builder steps are not merged into one page.** `/lesson-design`
rule 3 says parts that only mean something side by side belong side by side,
and a four-part frame is its own example of that. It does not reach here, and
the reason matters: **the builder is rehearsal, not instruction.** The shape
is taught whole on its own screen (change 2) and shown whole again on the
finish screen. In between, the reader is answering, one question at a time.

The half-built sentence was also tried on the builder steps and taken out on
purpose -- it read as a fourth thing to answer. That note is in `_Builder`.

**Six sorting sentences are not cut to four.** Recognition needs repetition,
each of the six carries a different giveaway, and the score's pass mark was
set against seven questions on 22 September 2026. Cutting two is a content
decision, not a structural one -- raise it separately if the drill feels long.

**The score step stays.** It is the feedback stage of instruct-model-rehearse-
feedback, it lives inside one sitting, and nothing about it is stored.

---

## For the next communication lesson

Work in this order. It is the order the screens are read in, and it stops a
lesson being written as a pile of good paragraphs.

1. Write the **one sentence** the reader should be able to say tomorrow.
2. Write screen 11 -- their line -- first. Everything before it exists to get
   them there.
3. Write screen 4 -- the swap. One situation, both ways.
4. Split screens 1 to 3 out of it: the subject, what goes wrong, what to do
   instead. Screens 2 and 3 take the SBI beats; screen 1 does not.
5. Write the sorting sentences, one giveaway each, none of them the sentence
   modelled on screen 4.
6. Write screen 12 last, from the source's own "how to practise" section.
7. Read every screen and ask what one thing it teaches.

docs.title: Low kind voice
docs.body:
# Somebody else, and you too

The **Low** face of the feeling picker. An original self-kindness script, about
**7 minutes** read at a slow pace with the pauses honoured.

Written 19 September 2026, and rewritten the same day. Nothing in it is taken
from any published script. The images -- a hand over the heart, kind words said
plainly, warmth sent outward before inward -- are common contemplative and
compassion-focused material with no owner. Every sentence here was written for
this file. See the rules section before changing a line.

Previously titled "Your own hand". The hand is still the anchor and the last
line, but it is no longer the main move, so the title moved with the script.

---

## Why this face is not a breathing screen and not a body scan

Low mood is kept going by **rumination** -- going over why you feel bad, again
and again. Nolen-Hoeksema's response-styles work is the long-running evidence
for it: a ruminative response to low mood predicts longer and worse episodes.

That rules out two obvious shapes:

| Shape | Why not |
| --- | --- |
| A long body scan | Slow, inward, unstructured attention is rumination's favourite shape. |
| "Sit with the sadness and look at it" | Noticing turns into chewing over, and the chewing is the mechanism. |

So attention in this script is either on **weight and warmth** (physical, no
story attached), on **somebody else**, or **wide** (the air, the feet, the
room). The script never asks why, and there is no line anywhere about what
caused this.

## Why self-kindness

Self-kindness is the right target. Low mood arrives loud with self-blame, and
low self-compassion tracks depression strongly across studies (MacBeth &
Gumley, *Clinical Psychology Review*, 2012). Kindness practices raise positive
feeling, which is the part of mood that goes flat (Fredrickson et al., 2008).

Neff's account of self-compassion has three parts: self-kindness, **common
humanity** -- the sense that this is a human thing rather than a fault in you --
and mindfulness. The first draft of this script had the first and the third and
nothing at all of the second, and that was the hole this rewrite fills.

Common humanity matters most for exactly this reader. Low mood says *it is only
me, and I am broken*. Warm words alone do not answer that. Another person in the
script does.

## Why the kindness goes outward first

The reader wishes an easy day on somebody they care about, and only then are
they included in the same words.

| Reason | Evidence or mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Aiming kindness at yourself stings | Gilbert's fear-of-compassion work finds that fear highest in people who are low and self-critical. Neff calls the sting backdraft. |
| Wishing well on somebody else is easy | It is the standard clinical route in. Neff & Germer's MSC and Gilbert's CFT both start warm attention on another and turn it inward afterwards. |
| It supplies common humanity | The other person is having their own day. That is the bridge, and it is the ingredient the first draft lacked. |

**The first draft rejected loving-kindness outright, and that rejection no
longer holds.** It was rejected for three reasons. The outward-first order fixes
one of them, and the other two are fixed by wording rather than by dropping the
shape:

| Original objection | What is done about it |
| --- | --- |
| Aiming kindness at yourself stings | Solved by the order. The reader is warm before they are included. |
| "Bring someone you love to mind" is a recall task | Cut the search. "Whoever turns up first" removes the rummaging and the ranking. |
| Warmth becomes the reader's job | The wishes carry no "for you" and are never checked. The reader says words, and never has to produce a feeling. |

**What is still rejected is the loving-kindness machinery**: the set phrases
("may I be happy, may I be safe"), the rings of people ending in a difficult
person, and the requirement to feel anything. The evidence for classic
loving-kindness is also thinner than its reputation -- meta-analyses (Galante
2014; Zeng 2015) find good effects on positive feeling and self-compassion, and
only small-to-moderate effects on depression, from small studies.

## The kindness arrives, it is not generated

This is still the decision the script turns on.

| Loving-kindness | Here |
| --- | --- |
| The reader generates the warmth | The reader says plain words, and their own palm supplies the warmth |
| The kind phrases are aimed at the self first | They are aimed outward first, then widened to include the self |
| Failure is possible | There is nothing to produce and nothing is checked |

**The screen carries an orb, and no line names it.** This script closes the
reader's eyes at part 1 and then keeps attention on weight, warmth and words,
so there is nobody watching after the fourth line. A character on screen would
be a performance to an empty room, and a line asking the reader to imagine
somebody beside them is a task -- and a cruel one if their answer is nobody.

**The rule is app-wide and it is not about this script.** Anything that closes
the reader's eyes, or turns attention onto body sensation, carries the orb.
Anything that shows the reader a posture to copy -- the tighten script, the
breathing pacer -- carries the character, because there the point is that she
is looked at. The two never share a screen: two things moving on two clocks is
what the breathing halo rule exists to prevent.

The earlier version of this section put the character here, and there was a
companion brief, `low-day-animation.md`, giving her seven minutes of poses.
Both are deleted. Do not rebuild either from this paragraph.

## Heard, and read while the recordings are missing

Same rules as `wound-up-tighten-and-stop.md`, with one change:

- **Closed eyes are asked for, and the words stay on screen anyway.** The 39
  recordings are not made yet, so the band is currently the only copy of the
  script. "Close your eyes." is an invitation, not a lock: somebody who keeps
  them open follows every line, and no line is hidden behind the instruction.
  Nothing at the end asks the reader to open them.
- **No line may name the screen, the voice, or the sound.** That is also why
  the widening section uses air, feet and space rather than sounds in the room.
- **Pauses carry both modes.** Heard, a pause is silence. Read, it is how long
  the line stays before the next one arrives.
- **Every line fits one glance.** The longest is fourteen words -- D1, "Now
  bring one hand up, and rest it on the middle of your chest." This said
  eleven until 20 September 2026, when the count was checked against the
  recording script and found wrong. Fourteen is the ceiling, not a target.

## The shape

| Part | Job | Lines | Approx |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0. Opening | Name the method, say why the order, hand control over. | 4 | 0:28 |
| 1. Settling | Arrive. Close the eyes. Let one breath out. | 7 | 0:44 |
| 2. Held | Whatever is under you takes the weight. | 4 | 0:41 |
| 3. Somebody else | The four wishes go outward, where they are easy. | 7 | 1:00 |
| 4. Your own hand | Warm touch. The hinge between outward and inward. | 3 | 0:37 |
| 5. And you too | The same four wishes, now including the reader. | 9 | 1:25 |
| 6. Wider | Attention goes out, off the chest and off the story. | 3 | 0:36 |
| 7. Leaving | Say it is over, and ask nothing. | 6 | 0:43 |

Forty-three lines and **43 takes**. Every line is its own recording: the two
sets of wishes are different words, so nothing is reused. About **6:16**. `[pause Ns]` is a held silence, not a read
line.

**The clock that matters is not the total. It is how long until the first kind
word**, because the kind words are the exercise and everything before them is
preamble. It was 2:41 on the morning of 20 September 2026 and it is 2:24 now.
Three lines were cut for that number alone.

Where the 2:24 goes, if it needs to come down again:

| Before the first wish | Takes |
| --- | --- |
| 0. Opening | 0:28 |
| 1. Settling | 0:44 |
| 2. Held | 0:42 |
| 3. Somebody else, up to the first wish | 0:30 |

Part 2 is the one to argue with next. It is four lines of weight with 8, 8 and
12 second silences, and it is doing real work -- the reader stops holding
themselves up -- but it is the largest block between opening the screen and
hearing anything kind.

**Seven minutes, not ten.** The mountain script can run ten and a half because
it is opened by somebody calm who chose to sit down. Low mood comes with poor
task persistence, so length here is a real risk of abandonment.

**Rewritten 20 September 2026, and it did not get longer.** Four things were
added -- an opening, a cued out-breath, the breath handed back, and a proper
closure -- and three lines were cut to pay for them:

| Cut | Why |
| --- | --- |
| "You are allowed to feel exactly what you feel." (part 3) | Aimed at the reader, in the one part whose whole job is to aim outward. Part 5 says it again, better, as "exactly this much". |
| "Your feet are heavy, and your hands are resting." (part 7) | Part 6 had just said both, two lines earlier. |
| "Nothing is finished, and nothing has to be." (part 7) | The new opening says "Nothing here has to be finished" first. |
| "Right now, somebody else is feeling exactly this." (part 5) | Sent attention back out to a stranger two lines after it finally arrived at the reader. See the rule below. |
| "There is nothing to answer." (part 3) | The script talking about itself -- reassurance about a task nobody was set. |
| "So these words go to somebody you care about first." (part 0) | The script promising a thing it does a minute later. Part 3 does it better by doing it. |
| "Then they come back to you." (part 0) | Same fault, and part 5 does it better. See the note on what the foreshadowing was worth. |
| "Whoever turns up first. A person, or an animal." (part 3) | An extra beat in front of the kindness. The guard it carried now lives in the verb of the line above it. |
| "Feel how much room there is around you." (part 6) | Three "Feel..." lines is a group; four is a checklist. It was also the only one asking for something the reader cannot touch -- air, feet and a hand are contact, "how much room" is a judgement about space made with the eyes shut. |
| "Let yourself be heavy on it." (part 2) | Asked for a state, not an action. Being heavy is not something a body does on command, and the likeliest guess -- pressing down -- is effort, which is the opposite of the instruction. |
| "Nothing has to be lifted right now." (part 2) | Nothing was being lifted, so it answered a question nobody had, and "lifted" points at no part of the body. |
| "You are allowed to feel exactly this much." (part 5) | "Exactly this much" is a quantity, and a quantity invites the reader to measure what they have got -- on the one screen built around not going over your own state. |
| "It is a human way to feel." (part 5) | "A human way to feel" is a construction, not a sentence. It makes the feeling a category of thing, which is work to do with the eyes shut. |
| "This is your own hand." (part 4) | The script admiring its own idea. The reader already knows whose hand it is. |
| "It has been warm all day." (part 4) | The same, one line later. The palm is already warm -- that is why the hand is the anchor -- so saying it again turns a sensation into a point being made. |

---

## 0. Opening

People call this loving kindness.

[pause 2s]

It is easier to be kind to a friend than to yourself.

[pause 3s]

Breathe normally the whole way through.

[pause 3s]

You can stop whenever you want. Nothing here has to be finished.

[pause 4s]

## 1. Settling

Find a position you could stay in for a while.

Close your eyes.

[pause 5s]

Let your spine be long, and let your shoulders drop.

Rest your hands wherever they land.

When your next breath comes, let it out slowly.

[pause 6s]

It is a low day.

You do not have to explain it to anyone.

[pause 10s]

## 2. Held

Feel whatever is under you, holding your weight.

It is doing all the work.

[pause 8s]

Let your weight sink down into it.

[pause 8s]

You can stop holding yourself up.

[pause 12s]

## 3. Somebody else

Now let somebody you care about come to mind.

[pause 6s]

They are somewhere else right now, having their own day.

[pause 8s]

Some simple kind words for them.

[pause 5s]

May you be safe.

[pause 3s]

May you be well.

[pause 3s]

May you be gentle with yourself.

[pause 3s]

May you have some peace, whatever today brings.

[pause 10s]

## 4. Your own hand

Now bring one hand up, and rest it on the middle of your chest.

[pause 5s]

Let it sit there with some weight.

[pause 8s]

Feel the warmth of your palm coming through.

[pause 12s]

## 5. And you too

Now somebody who has had this feeling all day.

[pause 5s]

That is you.

[pause 8s]

Now say them for yourself.

[pause 5s]

May I be safe.

[pause 3s]

May I be well.

[pause 3s]

May I be gentle with myself.

[pause 3s]

May I have some peace, whatever today brings.

[pause 12s]

You are allowed to feel like this.

[pause 10s]

This is part of being human.

[pause 10s]

## 6. Wider

Now let your hand come down, and rest it wherever it lands.

[pause 8s]

Feel the air on your face.

[pause 8s]

Feel the weight of your feet.

[pause 10s]

## 7. Leaving

Your breath is coming and going on its own.

[pause 6s]

This is how it is today.

[pause 8s]

Stay as long as you want.

[pause 8s]

When you are ready, let your eyes come back to the room.

Your hand can go back there whenever you want.

You can close this page when you are done.

---

## The rules, with the versions that were rejected

Each rule below cost something to find. The wrong version is kept so the rule
does not get quietly undone later.

### The person comes to mind, and is never searched for

"Now let somebody you care about come to mind."

This is the one place the script goes near memory at all, and it does so by
explicit decision. **A named person is worth the cost**: a real person the
reader cares about produces warmth that a stranger does not, and the warmth is
the whole engine of the turn in part 5.

**The guard against searching is the verb, and on 20 September 2026 it became
the only guard.** "Whoever turns up first." followed this line and was cut --
it was one more beat in front of the kindness on a script whose whole problem
is how long that takes. What it was protecting against survives, because "let
somebody come to mind" was always carrying it too:

| Verb | What the reader does |
| --- | --- |
| **Let** somebody come to mind | Waits. Somebody arrives. |
| **Bring** somebody to mind | Goes and gets one. |
| **Think of** somebody | Picks, which means ranking the people they love with their eyes shut. |

Change that verb and the guard is gone with it. That is the thing to watch in
this line, not its length.

| Rejected | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Bring to mind someone you love. | A search, and a ranking. Choosing from memory is time travel, which every script in this app bans. |
| Someone who has been good to you. Someone who makes things easier. | The elaboration is what turns an arrival into a task. This is the same fault the mountain script had, and the same fix. |
| Somebody, somewhere, is having a day like this one. | No recall at all, and safe -- but the warmth is thin, so the turn to self in part 5 has nothing to run on. |

### The person is alive, and elsewhere

"They are somewhere else right now, having their own day."

| Rejected | Why |
| --- | --- |
| *(nothing between the arrival and the kind words)* | Without this line, somebody who has died can turn up, and the script then sends kind words after them. |

The line is present tense and it names no death. It does the safety work
quietly, and it doubles as the common-humanity bridge -- they have their own
day, and so does the reader.

### The reader is included, never promoted

"Now somebody who has had this feeling all day. / That is you. / The same words
again, and they are for you as well."

| Rejected | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Now turn the kindness towards yourself. | Makes the self a new, harder section. A low reader then compares: they deserve it, I do not. That sharpens the self-blame this script exists to loosen. |
| And now, the hardest one. Yourself. | Predicts distress, and scores the attempt before it starts. |

Part 5 opens with the **same grammar** as part 3 -- "Now somebody who..." against
"Now let somebody...". The parallel is what makes the arrival of the reader feel
like inclusion rather than a promotion to a harder exercise.

### The version of you is today's, not childhood's

"Somebody who has had this feeling all day. / That is you."

The reader is offered a small step back from themselves before the kind words
land. That step is the mechanism: a self-critical person can refuse kindness
aimed at "me" and accept it aimed at "somebody who has had a day like that".

**The inner-child version was considered and rejected.** Picturing yourself as a
small child is the classic compassion-focused bridge, and it is used in CFT and
in schema therapy. Three things rule it out here:

| Problem | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Childhood is where the harm often is | For a real share of low readers, the child version of themselves is the scene of abuse, neglect or bullying. Inner-child work is done alongside a therapist, never by an app at two in the morning. |
| It is deep recall | Part 3's recall is light and present -- who do you care about, now. Childhood is the far past, and this app's scripts ban time travel. |
| It is rumination fuel | The whole face is built around Nolen-Hoeksema: no going back over your own story. A child self is an invitation to do exactly that. |
